articles.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
articles.description: The BBC meets the far-left protesters French President Emmanuel Macron says are trying to bring down the Republic.
articles.content:
'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left

ByKatya Adler
Europe Editor
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 06:01 GMT
Updated 13:09 GMT

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).

Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.

Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.

"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.

"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."

"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.

They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.

I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.

They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."

How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?

They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.

French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.

Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.

"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.

"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.

"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."

When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.

Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.

There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.

While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?

All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."

"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."

I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".

Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.

"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."

You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.

"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.

"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"

How can you say that, I want to know?

"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.

But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.

"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.

Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.

Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.

The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.

France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.description: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
articles.content:
Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat

ByMadeline Halpert
  • Published
    22 November 2026
Updated 23 November 2026 13:02 GMT

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

  • View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.

Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx two years ago by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

articles.title: Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
articles.description: The government blames overcrowding, poor maintenance, and missing life jackets for boat accidents.
articles.content:
Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy

ByMakuochi Okafor, BBC Africa, Reporting fromLagos and Ondiro Oganga
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 11:38 GMT
Updated 12:43 GMT

Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.

Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.

The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.

Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.

The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.

Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.

Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.

"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.

"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.

  • Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening?

    • Published
      20 July

Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.

"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.

There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.

The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.

"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.

In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.

He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.

Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.

In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

articles.title: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
articles.description: Democrats have currently flipped 47 House seats and could flip 49 total. And, climate change talks at COP31 ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest conference in the summit's history.
articles.content:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.

Julianna Conley/NPR

Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.

  • 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now.
Sponsor Message

Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.

  • 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says.

Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.

Sponsor Message
  • 🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says.

Books We Love

NPR

NPR's annual reading guide, Books We Love, is back with more than 380 new recommendations from staff and trusted critics. This year's picks span a range of genres, including fiction, cookbooks, children's reads, poetry and science fiction. Don't worry if it looks overwhelming; the interactive filters will help you narrow down your list and find your next great read. And why stop at this year's reads? The Books We Love archive has 14 years of recommendations, so you can discover more than 4,700 amazing books, all in one place. This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today.

Behind the story

by Maria Godoy, senior science and health editor and correspondent

Clinical services supervisor Dale Weiser poses for a portrait at the Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption

Daniel Vasta for NPR

People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.

Sponsor Message

Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.

So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.

Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."

Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here.

3 things to know before you go

Bottles of Roundup weed killer are displayed on a shelf at a Home Depot store on June 25, 2026 in North Hollywood, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America hide caption

Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America
  1. Bayer could pay up to $7.25 billion to settle lawsuits alleging that its weed-killer Roundup caused cancer. A Missouri judge gave final approval to the nationwide settlement.
  2. South Africa's grassroots program Read Alex is tackling a children's literacy crisis and inspiring kids to write. The initiative culminated in a book launch for an anthology titled From Gomora to the World, showcasing stories written by children.
  3. Orchestra Noir transforms 2000s hip-hop and R&B classics into high-energy, choreographed symphonic shows. Beyond delivering performances, the all-Black ensemble creates a cultural bridge through their post-show ritual, when musicians meet with their multigenerational audiences.

articles.title: Next data accessed in cyber breach
articles.description: The fashion retailer says there is no evidence customers' personal data was compromised.
articles.content:
Next data accessed in cyber breach

  • Published
    23 November 2026, 12:34 GMT

Next has said that some of its data has been accessed in a cyber breach affecting a third-party online supplier.

The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.

The firm - which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire - said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".

"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.

"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.

"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."

The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness", and working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.

Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.

In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account, leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.

The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.

In 2025 Marks & Spencer suffered from a major cyber-attack, which forced it to stop all online sales for about six weeks and led to some empty shelves in shops.

Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.

Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

articles.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
articles.description: Public sector workers have been hit by delays to pension payments, in a scheme overseen by Capita since last year.
articles.content:
Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure

  • Published
    23 November 2026, 10:46 GMT
Updated 11:24 GMT

Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

  • Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules

    • Published
      29 October

Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m.

This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions.

Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation".

The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health.

BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga, and left in financial hardship.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments.

"The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair."

'Capita needs to steady the ship'

Until the end of November 2025, the scheme was administered by a company called MyCSP.

The contract was taken over by Capita on 1 December, in a seven-year deal worth £239m.

"Capita inherited an enormous backlog of cases which needed addressing and failed to deliver on the promised automation, AI and digital tools needed to manage the 1.7 million members," said Russ Mould, investment director at investment platform AJ Bell.

"Efforts to fix the problems failed and government deadlines came and went, leading to the withholding of milestone payments, with the National Audit Office probing the contract.

"Capita needs to steady the ship quickly, and hope that the modest recent improvements in service levels on the civil service scheme can be built upon."

articles.title: The wind and the song: the treachery of AI
articles.description: As AI learns to look, talk and think ever more like us, this short film asks how we can stay fully human alongside it- by Aeon VideoWatch on Aeon
articles.content:
From finding human figures in the stars to creating prehistoric cave art, we’ve been anthropomorphising our world for millennia. Now, machine-learning technologies can generate photorealistic images, synthetic voices that laugh and pause for breath, and chatbots that crush the Turing test. We’re seeing the first generation in history for whom the line between humans and their representations could all but vanish.

In this video essay for the digital publication Fully Human, the UK animator and filmmaker Lewis Heriz interrogates where this is taking us. We inevitably build our world through symbols, he says, but the hall-of-mirrors reality we’re rapidly creating may be leading us down a perilous path. However, he argues, we’re not without agency. Instead of submitting to a world where data and people are indistinguishable, we should be thinking critically and imaginatively about how we might use AI in ways that preserve our humanity.

articles.title: A colossal oscillation
articles.description: El Niño has upended global weather, shaping the fate of societies, for millennia. Is this past a clue to a turbulent future?- by Dagomar DegrootRead on Aeon
articles.content:
Listen to this essay

26 minute listen

As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

It’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

The past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño’s future on a warming planet.

A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

It’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.

When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).

El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific

Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.

The modern version of El Niño seems easy to define. It’s a dramatic warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean – a warming that’s confined to the tropics, lasts for many months, and tends to peak around the end of the year. It transfers a stupendous quantity of heat and moisture into the atmosphere, which the tropical jet stream redistributes, reshuffling weather patterns from one region to another.

But what causes these recurring warmings of Pacific Ocean water? And how, exactly, do they affect regional weather patterns?

Only recently have scientists been able to answer those questions. It turns out that El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific Ocean, known as the Southern Oscillation. When air is tightly packed together over the eastern Pacific – when atmospheric pressure there is high, in other words – and when it’s low over the western Pacific, the pressure difference reinforces persistent winds that blow west along the equator.

These trade winds, as they’re called, can push so much warm surface water into the tropics of the western Pacific that they allow deeper, colder water to reach the top of the eastern Pacific. This is called La Niña. But when the difference in Pacific Ocean pressure dips, the trade winds falter, and the warm water of the western Pacific surges east. This we call El Niño.

Scientists have learned that the Southern Oscillation involves reinforcing relationships, known as feedbacks, between the air and sea. Usually, hot water in the western Pacific evaporates in towering storms, releasing heat. The air flows east, cools down, grows denser, falls, then surges back to the west, warming up.

This pattern, known as the Walker Circulation, strengthens the pressure differences of the Southern Oscillation and fuels the trade winds. But during an El Niño, warm water, evaporation and rains shift to the eastern Pacific, weakening transpacific differences in pressure and, in turn, the trade winds. This pattern helps explain the most important weather associated with El Niño: torrential rains across parts of the Western Hemisphere, and drought in Australasia.

Today, El Niño seems less like an event, and more like one end of a seesaw that perpetually teeters across the Pacific. But why does the seesaw behave as it does? There is still no scientific consensus, but the historical traces of both human societies and the natural world provide us with clues.

The most important questions about El Niño concern its impacts on global weather patterns – or in other words, the teleconnections that form between the warming of the equatorial Pacific and droughts, floods, storms or heatwaves around the world.

These teleconnections are usually presented as predictable and consistent from one El Niño to the next. They’re visualised in maps that supposedly depict how regional temperatures or precipitation change as El Niño intensifies in the Pacific Ocean

But no two El Niño events have exactly the same teleconnections. One reason is that the extent, intensity and duration of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific differs from one El Niño to the next. Another is that El Niño is only one of many influences on regional weather, and its effects generally weaken with distance from the tropical Pacific.

Because El Niño’s impacts on regional weather are never identical, it’s impossible to predict exactly how a future El Niño will impact most of the world’s people and ecosystems. But it’s even harder to piece together the history of El Niño before the beginning of the 20th century, when ships began to regularly measure sea-surface temperatures. And it’s harder still before the middle of the 19th century, when scientists began to systematically gather data from rain gauges where El Niño reliably generates heavy precipitation.

Decades of research now reveals broad patterns in El Niño history that could give a rough sense of what’s in store

It’s a challenge, but not impossible. Climatologists – and a handful of historians and geographers – estimate the timing, strength and impacts of El Niño before the mid-19th century by consulting what they call the ‘archives of society’ and the ‘archives of nature’.

The archives of society were created by the people of the past. They include surviving texts that describe weather directly, such as the logbooks that sailors wrote aboard ships. They also include diverse sources of evidence – not only documents but also artefacts, ruins, even oral traditions – that record human activities so dependent on the weather that they can serve as proxies for it.

Unlike the archives of society, the archives of nature were created by Earth itself (even if they are, of course, interpreted by people). These archives are parts of the natural world that responded either to changes in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean, or to the regional extremes in temperature and precipitation that can be associated with those changes. The responses leave a mark in natural archives, changing the composition of growth rings in trees or corals, for example. Each mark serves as a proxy for El Niño conditions in the distant past.

Neither societal nor natural archives can provide direct measurements of sea-surface temperatures or weather, so histories of El Niño are inevitably full of uncertainty. Trees, for example, can only grow (or stop growing) so much. It’s one reason why their rings can’t precisely measure the strength of past El Niño events (and one reason why we can’t easily pin down whether this year’s El Niño really is the strongest in a millennium).

Still, decades of research can now reveal three broad patterns in El Niño history that could give us a rough sense of what’s in store – not only in the coming year, but in our future on a warming world.

Above all, El Niño shaped humanity’s past by suddenly changing where water was available, how much there was, and how people could use it.

The foundations of human life – food, shelter and movement – depend to varying degrees on water. Human populations can use water in many different ways, so they have learned to thrive in very different environments. But it seems to have been much harder for them to adapt to the sudden disruptions in water that a strong El Niño – or that a trend towards stronger El Niño conditions overall – could bring about.

This is the first pattern in El Niño’s human history.

We can already see its outlines a little more than 4,000 years ago, when the first states and empires established themselves. At that time, El Niño conditions seem to have grown more frequent, intense and long-lasting. The reason may have been a multimillennial cycle in the wobble of Earth’s rotation that altered the amount of sunlight associated with different seasons, weakening the trade winds.

It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges

Natural and societal archives suggest that some communities withered as El Niño intensified. In Peru, for example, populations appear to have deserted temple mounds, giant platforms that supported elaborate buildings and plazas. It’s easy to imagine that torrential floods sparked by strong El Niño conditions made it impossible to maintain these structures. But archaeological evidence hints at other changes that might have been partly responsible for population movements, including new trade networks and newly cultivated plants. How much can the coincidence of two trends really tell us about causation?

Maybe quite a lot, if similar coincidences pop up elsewhere. And it seems they do. A little under 3,000 years ago, for example, settlers established a community at Teouma, on the island of Efate in today’s Vanuatu. Chemical traces of human waste and leaves in nearby swamp sediments show that the settlers cultivated taro, a root vegetable, during a period of increasing rainfall. By around 2,600 years ago, however, a trend towards stronger or more frequent El Niño conditions seems to have made local rainfall more erratic. The trend appears to correlate with a decline in settlement and cultivation on Efate.

You’ll notice a lot of conditional language about possible changes and potential correlations. Deep history is like that. Natural and societal archives can let us identify probable trends, figure out roughly when they happened, and craft convincing theories for how one trend caused another. It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges that compels us to re-date a trend, or propose another cause for it.

In general, evidence from the archives of nature and society is more abundant and precise the closer it dates to our present. Evidence from the previous millennium lets us identify not just trends in human and El Niño history, but discrete events.

Catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions

By the 16th century, for example, cave formations, tree rings and reports written by government officials let us reconstruct the likely impacts of individual El Niño years on the Indian summer monsoon. They reveal a series of devastating droughts across India in the late 16th century, the middle and end of the 17th century, and the late 18th century.

It may be that a series of explosive volcanic eruptions were partly responsible for these droughts. The cooling effect of the sulphur they launched into the upper atmosphere altered temperature differences between latitudes, and between land and water. These differences in temperature help create the winds that bring monsoon rains; when they changed, the rains did too.

But the droughts also coincided with El Niño conditions. In fact, there may be a connection, because the new wind patterns created by powerful eruptions seem to warm the eastern Pacific, relative to the west. Regardless, El Niño can also weaken the Indian monsoon by shifting warm water and rising air eastward across the tropical Pacific.

When the monsoon rains failed, harvests could too. Of course, rural populations and states had many ways of protecting themselves. Wells and granaries stored water and seeds, for instance, while trade networks could allow for emergency food imports. Still, these systems broke down when droughts lasted too long – and especially when states waged war.

In some El Niño events and in some parts of India, droughts provoked widespread famine only when armies demanded food from the already depleted countryside. In other Indian regions, the death toll soared when widespread malnutrition joined migration from drought-stricken regions to encourage the spread of epidemic disease. All told, catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions across 16th-, 17th- and 18th-century India.

Everywhere El Niño sparked extreme weather, communities suffered. Yet some prospered at their expense, and this is the second pattern we can discern in El Niño’s history.

The collapse of China’s Ming dynasty in the 17th century seems to provide a striking example. Growth rings in trees and corals indicate that El Niño conditions repeatedly contributed to a weakening of the East Asian monsoon in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. At first, droughts afflicted both northeastern China – home of the loosely connected Jurchen peoples – and northern China, the Ming heartland.

In the diverse environments of northeastern China, the Jurchen hunted, fished and farmed, a varied subsistence strategy that gave them some protection from drought. They also raided across the Great Wall into Ming territory, where they seized stockpiled grain. Eventually, droughts intensified in northern China, where soaring food prices and famine helped to destabilise the Ming regime. But drought seems to have yielded to above-average rainfall in Jurchen territories. Food provided by plentiful rain may have aided efforts to consolidate Jurchen communities into a united ‘Manchu’ state that was strong enough to exploit the Ming dynasty’s weakness, conquer China, and establish a new Qing dynasty.

Indeed, conquest and colonialism created a means by which the impacts of El Niño could be amplified for some communities, but alleviated or even exploited for others. This redistribution of vulnerability was never clearer or more catastrophic than in the late 19th century, when exceptionally strong El Niño conditions coincided with a global age of imperialism.

The exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place

In 1876, drought spread across India, then intensified with a strong El Niño in 1877-78. It was the heyday of the British Raj. Colonial officials had upended lives and livelihoods in many Indian farming communities by forcing them to plant cash crops such as tea or cotton. Now, there wasn’t enough food to go round. What grain could be harvested was either redirected from the poorest communities to areas where people could pay more, or exported out of India by colonial administrators who scorned market interventions.

Tens of millions died in the ensuing famines.

Similar tragedies played out wherever El Niño sparked drought in the late 19th century, though the exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place. In Eritrea and Ethiopia, for instance, Italian invaders arrived with cattle infected by rinderpest, a deadly disease that spread to local cattle before the arrival of another strong El Niño in 1890-91. Widespread mortality among cattle intensified food shortages, as did the arrival of immense locust swarms.

Perhaps a third of Ethiopia’s population perished.

The United States, however, often benefitted from El Niño conditions. As worldwide droughts drove up grain prices in 1877-78, US farmers exported enormous quantities of wheat to Europe. The resulting inflow of gold-backed credit strengthened US finances, and helped the government manage its Civil War debts. A century later, during another strong El Niño in 1972, the collapse of the Peruvian anchovy fishery, owing both to warming water and years of overfishing, deprived poultry producers of fishmeal. But that allowed US farmers to profit by planting soy, a substitute. In the even stronger 1982-83 event, torrential rains devastated California and other southern states, but overall, the US economy received a powerful stimulus from mild winter weather.

It was around this time – the late 20th century – that scientists and journalists created the modern concept of El Niño as a global event that recurred every few years to cause predictable disasters. This is the third pattern in our history. El Niño is not just an environmental reality; it’s also a cultural reality: a manufactured threat that is a unique product of our time.

In some respects, that threat was a creation of the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). During the IGY, a global campaign to observe Earth and near-Earth space served as an arena for scientific and technological competition between the US and Soviet governments. The IGY fortuitously coincided with an El Niño, and unprecedented observations helped scientists begin to understand the true dimensions of Pacific Ocean warming.

It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways

Cold War politics continued to shape El Niño science. The 1959 Cuban Revolution joined the growing importance – for poultry farmers – of the Peruvian anchovy fishery to spur US support for collaborations between US and Latin American scientists. These collaborations, many of which focused on the study of El Niño, were supposed to demonstrate the value of partnership with US institutions.

When navies deployed nuclear submarines to reinforce newly developed nuclear arsenals, they began to fund oceanographic research partly to better understand the underwater battlespace. Until then, oceanographers had been able to visit marine environments only occasionally, in ships. Beginning in the 1950s, new funds and technology allowed them to deploy instruments to monitor environments continuously, for months or years at a time.

The launch of Sputnik 1 during the IGY also heralded a new age in which weather satellites kept the oceans under constant supervision from above. And computer models soon seemed capable of forecasting not just global warming, but also the state of the Southern Oscillation. By the early 1980s, prominent scientists believed that El Niño could finally be predicted months in advance.

Yet the strong El Niño of 1982-83 came as a shock to the overwhelming majority of meteorologists and oceanographers. It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways, and each had distinct impacts on regional weather patterns. Because the unanticipated El Niño led to floods, droughts and storms that killed thousands of people, inflicted billions of dollars in damage, and cost the global economy trillions in estimated lost growth, scientists redoubled their efforts to forecast El Niño and its teleconnections.

The concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media

In 1985, the World Meteorological Organization – a United Nations agency – launched a decade-long project to scatter ocean-monitoring buoys across the tropical Pacific. Scientists also began to use both societal and natural archives to reconstruct the deep history of El Niño. In early 1997, they had learned enough to successfully predict another ocean warming months before it happened. Scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) alerted US journalists, and they created a media sensation: an El Niño reimagined as a looming, worldwide catastrophe.

It’s ironic that American journalists developed this threatening new view of El Niño. In the US, the economic benefits of the 1997-98 El Niño would again far outweigh the damage. But the concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Since the 19th century, US reporters had thrilled audiences by portraying natural phenomena as sensational, often threatening events – events that could be understood only by plucky scientists. A close but routine approach of a comet or planet to Earth, for example, became a brush with death recorded by swashbuckling scientists in far-flung observatories.

It was journalism that resonated in a culture shaped by religious concepts of a purifying apocalypse. And it helps explain why, in the 20th century, the scientific investigation of changes in the atmosphere – not just global warming, but also nuclear winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, and even the potential consequences of asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions – relied on US funding and institutions, while coming to particularly alarm US citizens.

Now, some US journalists used the Spanish name of El Niño to conjure an image of a foreign menace that several compared to migrants from South America. As the 1997-98 El Niño warmed into the strongest event since the 19th century, ‘Blame it on El Niño’ and ‘Don’t blame me, blame El Niño!’ were common slogans on everything from bumper stickers to T-shirts. That was true even though scientists couldn’t predict exactly how El Niño would affect weather in most parts of the world, let alone how populations would react.

It was in 1997 that today’s understanding of El Niño – part Cold War relic, part scientific achievement, and part media monster – was born.

The patterns in El Niño’s past teach us that the warming of the tropical Pacific can be disastrous for communities exposed to droughts and floods. But they also reveal that El Niño disasters are caused less by the severity of weather extremes, and more by the brutality of how some communities are exploited by others. They suggest that today’s imagined El Niño – a global threat, with predictable impacts on weather – is less an accurate reflection of reality than a creation of modern science, media and geopolitics.

In the coming years and decades, it’s likely that El Niño’s impacts on populations will be shaped primarily by human relationships and ideas, not by nature. But human actions now include greenhouse gas pollution on such a scale that Earth has warmed by about 1.5°C, relative to its average temperature in the late 19th century. This pollution is supercharging the impacts of El Niño on weather. Heatwaves are growing hotter, and intensifying evaporation means droughts are getting worse. Partly because a warm atmosphere holds more water, downpours are ever more intense.

Global warming doesn’t seem capable of ending the Southern Oscillation, and with it the age-old seesaw of El Niño and La Niña. Still, it could lead to even more intense El Niño events that cause even more extreme weather.

It’s never been more urgent to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. But El Niño’s past also teaches us a deeper lesson about adapting to climatic extremes. Today, the world seems increasingly shaped by renewed great power competition: by militarism and colonial relationships between superpowers and their patrons. History suggests that such a world could be one in which millions die unnecessarily, not just through war but in preventable climate disasters.

It’s a warning from the past that today’s governments would be wise to heed, as El Niño reshapes environments from one end of the world to another in the months and years to come.

articles.title: South East Water reports loss after supply issues
articles.description: South East Water records a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September.
articles.content:
South East Water reports loss after supply issues

ByHsin-Yi Lo
South East
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 10:19 GMT

South East Water has reported a half-year loss after penalties and £29m of costs following disruption to water supplies over the summer.

The company, which serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England, recorded a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September, compared with a profit of £18.2m during the same period last year.

In July, regulator Ofwat ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after supply interruptions hit customers across Kent and Sussex which affected more than 286,000 customers.

The company spent £29m responding to further supply interruptions during summer heatwaves in Kent and Sussex.

This included providing bottled water, setting up emergency water stations and compensating customers.

South East Water said it had set aside £14.6m in its latest financial results to cover the redress package.

The company supplies water to customers in Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

Hosepipe bans remain in force across all areas supplied by South East Water.

'Signs of improvement'

In October, it was forced to ask shareholders for £50m after warning earlier in the year that it required additional funding in order to stay afloat.

The company said there were "early signs of improvement" following changes to its leadership team and plans for a "significant transformation" of the business.

Earlier this year, John Halsall was appointed chief executive after former chief executive David Hinton and chair Chris Train stepped down.

The departures followed criticism from MPs who said they had "no confidence" in the company's leadership after a review of repeated supply outages.

Richard Morse is due to become chair of the company on 3 December, succeeding interim chair Lisa Clement.

South East Water said the initial signs were "encouraging", although it warned improvements would take time to become fully visible to customers.

A spokesperson for the company said: "We know that customers will not judge us on the number of initiatives we launch or the promises we make.

"They will judge us on whether their water supply is more reliable, whether we communicate better and whether we provide the right support when they need it – we look forward to providing the evidence in future results."

articles.title: Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?
articles.description: Poundland has a matter of days to find a buyer or face collapsing into administration. Why?
articles.content:
Poundland is facing collapse - what's gone wrong?

ByTom Espiner
Business reporter
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 00:22 GMT
Updated 10:09 GMT

The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

How have we got here?

Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."

She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."

However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.

Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.

So why is it facing administration?

Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

What future does Poundland have?

For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.

Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".

Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.

"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.

There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.

But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

articles.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
articles.description: Wellness influencers say mushroom supplements can help with your gut health, focus and immune system. Here is where research suggests there are some links.
articles.content:
Maria Fabrizio for NPR

Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.

Short Wave

This gas station drug acts like opioids. It's getting harder to buy

"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."

Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.

"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."

Sponsor Message

Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.

"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."

The claim

Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.

For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.

And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.

The evidence

Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.

Sponsor Message

Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."

Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."

Your Turn with Allison Aubrey

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.

In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.

"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.

Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.

Sponsor Message

"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."

Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.

Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."

The bottom line

In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.

And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."

Short Wave

How a viral video gave a huge boost to new gene therapy

Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.

"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."
