articles.title: K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
articles.description: A decade after first asking families about kindness, Sesame Workshop asked parents similar questions. They responded that their kids are getting kinder even as the wider world becomes less so.
articles.content:
The new season of Sesame Street focuses on kindness. Sesame Workshop hide caption

Sesame Workshop

Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.

Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' views on kindness from Sesame Workshop, the education nonprofit behind Sesame Street.

"Caregivers see the world as much more unkind to their young children than they did in 2016," says Kim Foulds, vice president of research and evaluation at Sesame Workshop, "but the reason to hope is that parents see their children as more kind, more empathetic, more resilient than they did in 2016."

Sponsor Message

The new "K is for Kind Study 2026" comes 10 years after the original "K is for Kind: A National Survey on Kindness and Kids," and it offers a remarkable glimpse at how families' feelings about kindness have shifted, in some cases dramatically, over a decade defined by the rise of social media and bitter political polarization.

NPR Ed

E Is For Empathy: Sesame Workshop Takes A Crack At Kindness

Monday's release also coincides with the debut of Sesame Street's 57th season, which will focus on kindness and compassion in action.

Let's start with that bad news: Compared to survey results from 2016, caregivers today have a much darker view of the world:

  • About 80% often worry the world is an unkind place for children. That's a nearly 11-percentage-point increase since 2016;
  • Fifty-four percent say kindness is not a priority for most people, a 10-point increase since 2016; and
  • On a scale of 1 to 5, caregivers give the average American a 2.8 for kindness. 

Taken together, the data shows a worrying shift in the way families perceive the world — as a place with more rough edges that is less attuned to the needs of their young children. To draw these conclusions, Sesame Workshop conducted 2,080 interviews in October with a nationally representative sample of caregivers of children ages 3-8 years old across all 50 states.

Sponsor Message

The good news, Foulds says, is that, while caregivers "are concerned about the division and unkindness they see in the wider world, their experience of their own children is much more immediate and hopeful."

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

This manifests in a few key ways. First, in parents' own values for their children:

  • Caregivers say they value their child being considerate (68%) over being smart (32%);
  • They value compassion (56%) over confidence (44%), a big swing of 8 percentage points compared to when the same question was asked in the 2016 survey; and
  • They value empathy (64%) over manners (36%) — an even bigger swing of 24 points compared to a decade ago.

In short, parents and caregivers say their values are shifting toward kindness. That shift, in turn, is showing up in the behaviors families say they're seeing from their kids.

  • A whopping 92% of caregivers rate their child highly for kindness, a 5-percentage point increase since 2016;
  • Some 74% of caregivers rate their child highly for resilience, a 12-point increase; 
  • And 56% gave their child a low anxiety rating, an 8-point improvement over 2016.

And that leads to what Foulds says was one of the most startling — and hopeful — results from the survey: 94% of caregivers said, when their child does something kind, they do it on their own, without encouragement or nudging.

"The child was seeing the opportunity to be kind themselves," Foulds says. "And I thought that was an incredibly beautiful, incredibly powerful finding to see how kindness is showing up in action in young children's lives."

These encouraging numbers come with one grain of salt: It's not unusual for caregivers to have a rosier view of their own children or their own local circumstances than of the wider world. In fact, this is a common phenomenon in education research, for example, where families often give America's schools low marks but high marks to their child's school and their child's teacher.

Sponsor Message

While this phenomenon likely influenced today's results, too, Sesame's twin surveys still offer a remarkable view of how caregivers' own views have shifted over the past decade.

What is kindness? The survey offers answers there, too. Caregivers talk about their children sharing in a way that requires them to give something up, connecting across languages and culture, making room for different abilities and including children who have been left out.

The survey also includes caregiver testimonials.

The parent of a 4-year-old told researchers, "He has a child in his class that is neurodivergent, which is different than him, and he is always helpful, always kind, always says 'Hi' whenever he sees this child for class and tries to be a good friend."

The parent of a 6-year-old told researchers, "My child was friends with an autistic child who is nonverbal. My child figured out a way to communicate with him, even though he could not express himself with words."

Children's Health

Sesame Street's effect on children

In the new survey, 85% of caregivers say it's "extremely important" to promote kindness, which is what Sesame Street's latest season will do when it debuts today on both Netflix and PBS KIDS.

"Each story really focuses on kindness, compassion, big feelings, and it's really designed to inspire children to carry the lessons beyond the screen," Foulds says. "We want the viewing to be the beginning of something, not the beginning and end."

In one scene from the new season, Muppets Elmo and Abby realize their choices have made a playmate feel left out and alone. They feel badly and decide to comfort and include him.

As one of the show's grown-ups reminds them, "One little help is all it takes."

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

articles.title: Catering giant to switch main share listing to US in further blow to UK
articles.description: A growing number of firms have been leaving the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.
articles.content:
Catering giant to switch main share listing to US in further blow to UK

ByMichael Race
Business reporter
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 09:54 GMT

Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange.

A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday.

Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations.

It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times, external, is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic.

North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn.

However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.

These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter.

Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells.

  • 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

    • Published
      8 October

  • Action urged to halt exodus of firms leaving UK

    • Published
      9 July 2025

The company was created during the Second World War after the Factories Canteen Order meant large manufacturing or munitions firms employing 250 people or more had an obligation to provide hot meals for workers.

Today, Compass operates across more than 25 countries and employs more than 600,000 people.

It is understood the group's proposed move to the US will have no impact on the number of UK employees and a consultation process with investors could take more than a year. It is expected to retain a secondary listing in London.

In a sign its listing could change, Compass changed the currency in which it trades its standard shares on the LSE from sterling to US dollars in April this year.

The boss of the LSE recently called on the government to do more to back homegrown companies and make the UK "more attractive" to invest in the domestic stock market.

Dame Julia Hoggett told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so.

"We need to take the handbrake off."

Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

articles.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
articles.description: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
articles.content:
Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict

ByBasillioh Rukanga
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 08:53 GMT

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

  • Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader

    • Published
      31 October

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

You may also be interested in:

  • DR Congo-Kenya rebel-group row rattles region

    • Published

  • Your phone, a rare metal and the war in DR Congo

articles.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.description: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
articles.content:
Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

ByJustin Rowlatt, Climate editor and Esme Stallard, Senior climate and science journalist, Reporting fromAntalya, Turkey
  • Published
    23 November 2026, 06:33 GMT

The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.

The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:

  • Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external

  • The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life

  • Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.

Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

  • Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

    • Published
      18 hours ago

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

COP31 had some good news

Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.

But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.

In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.

And some of those were agreed at the talks.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

The economics have been changing too.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.

As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.

Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".

That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.

"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".

The COP process needs to change

COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.

For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.

The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.

The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

COP collapses: What's the future for climate action?

The COP summit in Turkey has failed because of a row about even mentioning the cause of climate change. Is there a way the world can move forward with coordinated climate action?

Listen on Sounds

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.

This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.

It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.

On many of the procedural issues Camilla Born spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.

And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.

The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

articles.title: Househunter swaps Australia for Wales' most affordable town - where locals are struggling to buy
articles.description: The area has attracted investors and even a buyer from Australia, but locals struggle to afford homes.
articles.content:
Househunter swaps Australia for Wales' most affordable town - where locals are struggling to buy

ByStephen Fairclough and Tony Brown, BBC Wales, Reporting fromFerndale, Rhondda Cynon Taf
  • Published
    22 November 2026
Updated 23 November 2026 06:03 GMT

A house-hunter has moved 10,000 miles (16,000km) from Australia to Wales' most affordable town because the properties are so cheap.

James Brown, 56, spotted the three-bed house in Tylorstown, near Ferndale, Rhondda Cynon Taf, online for £80,000 and put an offer in.

"It's ideal if you're commuting, and everything's virtually on your doorstep, so a really affordable area to come to," he said.

But some people who live in Ferndale - dubbed Wales' most affordable town with an average property price of £116,200 - say they are still struggling to buy homes.

Zoopla says a typical home in Ferndale costs "less than twice the annual wages of two full-time workers".

The property selling website said its analysis shows this is the most affordable town in Wales.

Residents have described how they have had to travel to work in England to afford a home in the area, while an estate agent said the low prices attract investors and buy-to-rent landlords from outside south Wales.

Originally from Gloucester, when Brown moved back from Australia he decided to move to the south Wales valleys because of the property prices.

He said the equivalent property in his home region would have cost him £200,000.

Brown said: "It's definitely a lot of outside buyers buying properties in Wales which I suppose in some ways is not helping the local people get on the ladder, but like I said, the affordability is just unreal in south Wales."

Emma Weston, 36, who runs a café in Ferndale said she had to make the choice between using savings to invest in her business or buying a house.

"Obviously, I chose to keep my job and put the money here," she said.

My partner, he's an electrician, a good trade, I obviously manage a business.

"We still have money but there's nothing left in the pot whereby I can say we can save X-amount to put down to a deposit."

Weston knows property is more expensive elsewhere, but says Ferndale still does not feel affordable.

"I've lived outside of the valleys, therefore I can see the comparisons," she said.

"However, if you look at the cost of living crisis, which we're all facing, everything is just costing an absolute bomb."

Café customer Marcus, 31, took a job nearly 100 miles (165km) away in Somerset so he could afford a family home.

"Moving to my new job gave that opportunity to buy the house," he said.

Thomas said he liked the security of having his own home, and sees it as an investment for his children.

But he said: "I think if you were living in London, Reading... Birmingham... I'd say it is the easiest place to get a property because the house value here and there is completely different.

"For us, it's hard. For people coming into Wales is easy and is affordable."

Estate agent David Ricketts said the south Wales valleys are attractive to people outside the area.

"You're getting more for your money, there's less stress, there's a lower mortgage to pay and it's an area which I think will get better and better, it'll grow and you'd get a lovely welcome in any valleys town," he said.

Ricketts said some buyers were not necessarily looking to live there themselves.

"What you've got now is a situation, not only just to buy, you have investors coming in because they've realised that the rental yield is quite reasonable and that will only grow," he said.

"These are very attractive areas to live and also to be a landlord."

Donna Thomas, 41, rents in Maerdy with her partner and their three children.

They rent because a mortgage is too expensive.

"If we're happy where we are, why change that? Why go into an even more stressful situation rather than just stay where we are and make do with what we have?

"It would be more stress, and everything would be harder, the money wouldn't stretch as far and the thing is we want to give the girls the best life that we possibly can with what we have," she said.

Thomas said she was happy for investors to buy properties in the area and rent them back to locals.

She said: "It means that when you can't afford to get a mortgage on a house that you really like, if somebody else did buy it, and then rented it out to you, I would say that would be really good.

"I think I can't afford to get a mortgage on this house, but I really like this house, and now I'm renting it."

Chiropractor Ellie Thomas, 25, lives with her parents in Ferndale.

She is saving up for a deposit on a house near a city.

"I don't think I would want to live here," she said.

"I just feel like there's not much going on here. Most of the shops are shut. There's like one café, a few hairdressers, there's not really much."

However, she understands it was likely to be more expensive and harder to buy elsewhere.

"Obviously, it's a bit hard to find somewhere nice in the area you want for an affordable price," she said.

"It would be easier for me to live here.

"It's a lovely community, everyone knows each other, but it's just a bit far out of the way, and petrol is expensive now too."

articles.title: Burnham not ‘backtracking’ on creating closer links with EU, officials say
articles.description: Government wants to let trade deal ‘breathe a bit’, insiders say, after speculation No 10 is dialling back ambitionsAndy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs
articles.content:
Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs of an apparent slowdown in the timetable.

The prime minister has promised to set out options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, including the possibility of rejoining, saying last week that these would be outlined later in the year.

But speaking at Friday’s UK-EU summit after finalising a deal on reducing food and drink checks, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme, Burnham talked instead about “brainstorming” ideas with the EU for what comes next, with a timetable given of some months.

The apparent slowdown prompted speculation No 10 wants to dial back the political pressure and prevent his agenda being swamped by arguments about the EU, with campaign groups being formed before a possible debate about rejoining.

But after Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, talked warmly on Sunday about the benefits of more integration, government officials said this was still the aim after a “really positive” summit in which the EU side, they said, promised to be as helpful as possible with whatever comes next.

“There is no backtracking or pumping the brakes,” one said. “The government just wants to let this deal breathe a bit, and point to the benefits.”

Another official said: “There hasn’t been a timetable shift since the summit. It’s being considered alongside the domestic agenda and the 10-year plan.”

Burnham will seek to keep up the initiative from the summit with a visit on Monday to a branch of Morrisons, in part to see the supermarket chain’s efforts in employing young people, but also to push home his message that the deal on food checks will lower retail prices.

Also on Monday the prime minister is expected to brief the Commons on the summit and deal, where he will face a hostile reception from opposition parties, particularly Reform UK.

In a speech to the CBI conference on Monday, Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, will tell business leaders that rejoining the EU would be “a disaster” for the UK economy, and that his party would reverse the deal made in Brussels.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has been critical of Burnham’s negotiations, but noticeably less trenchant about the wider idea of smoothing trade links with Europe, part of a strategy to focus instead on subjects such as the economy and defence.

“Seamless trade benefits the UK, but it also benefits the EU,” she will say, according to an advance extract of her own speech to the CBI conference. “If we can make our trading relationship better, good. I’m all for working on a smarter deal.”

In contrast, Theresa May, who carried out the bulk of the Brexit negotiations with Brussels before being replaced by Boris Johnson, made a rare intervention on day-to-day politics to warn Burnham that rejoining would tie up his government for years.

She told the BBC: “That’s one of the reasons why I looked slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham was talking about – further negotiations of going into the EU.

“As a country, we voted for Brexit. When I was prime minister, I was very clear: we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is: people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.”

In his own interview with the BBC on Sunday, Miliband argued that closer links with the EU would mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels.

“At the moment, what the situation is is that we are essentially rule takers,” the foreign secretary said. “Businesses are rule takers if they want to sell into the European market. So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union, but at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms.”

He said this was “the worst of all worlds” and it meant there was a clear case to integrate more closely into EU markets.

Another reason for even closer ties, he said, was the transformed geopolitical order since 2016, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the US’s distancing from Europe under Donald Trump.
articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent

articles.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
articles.description: Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party groupEd Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a
articles.content:
Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

The group, coordinated by the all-party group on anti-corruption (APPG), said an improvement in corporate transparency in the overseas territories was essential after “years of broken promises and missed deadlines from certain jurisdictions, and despite repeated commitments to ending secrecy”.

They said some territories such as Gibraltar, Montserrat and St Helena had successfully opened corporate registers to the public.

But they called out the British Virgin Islands, saying it “in particular continues to let the British family down”. They said the Cayman Islands has raised its search fees to “prohibitive levels”, and Turks and Caicos have introduced huge fines for disclosing information from the register which they said was “undermining the entire purpose of open registers”.

They said that persistent engagement in good faith from the UK government has yielded few results, in the face of “outright disregard for the will of parliament”.

The BVI has a register launched this year which allows people to apply for access to ownership information if they have a “legitimate interest” such as investigating money laundering. A BVI Government spokesperson said: “We are proud of the BVI’s Legitimate Interest Access register introduced earlier this year, which allows for prompt, proportionate access, in line with international standards.

“We continue to work closely with the UK Government, delivering a major governance and regulatory reform programme to support global efforts combatting illicit finance, enforcing sanctions and recovering criminal assets - with significant progress recently recognised by the Financial Action Task Force.”

However, ahead of the meeting, the MPs including former Conservative Foreign Office minister Andrew Mitchell and Labour anti-corruption expert Phil Brickell are asking Miliband to lay an order in council mandating fully public registers of beneficial ownership in jurisdictions that continue to fail to meet their obligations.

They said it was important for UK national security “because continued secrecy undermines our ability to enforce sanctions and leaves us open to hostile state actors and criminal networks”. Second, they said developing countries continue to be destabilised and looted by kleptocrats using Britain’s own offshore financial centres to clean and stash their ill-gotten gains.

Parliament voted for open registers in 2018 and the UK government had expected public access registers to be in place in all overseas territories and crown dependencies by 2023. However, this deadline was not met.

While an order in council to mandate open registers was drafted in 2020, the government said that because there were “firm commitments” from the overseas territories to introduce public registers, the order would not be used. It said it would keep this decision under review.

Brickell, Labour chair of the APPG, said “it should never have come to this but every year of deliberate delay is another year in which kleptocrats, tax dodgers and money launderers can hide behind a British flag”.

“That is a stain on the reputation of our global family. This joint ministerial council must be the moment we finally draw a line under it.”

Mitchell, a Conservative vice-chair of the APPG and former development secretary, said: “When parliament voted for public registers in 2018, it was not making a polite request. It was the clear, cross-party will of the House of Commons, and it should have been respected.

“Instead, money stolen from some of the poorest people on earth is still being hidden behind anonymous companies in British jurisdictions. That money should be building hospitals and schools. It is paying for yachts and mansions instead, and the price is measured in lives. The British family has been patient for long enough. The foreign secretary has the power to act, and I urge him to use it.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Security is the first duty of any government. Hostile states and malign actors can exploit opaque corporate structures like those in the British Virgin Islands to hide their assets and support activity that threatens our national security.

“Ministers are actively considering how best to ensure that, where the risks are greatest, law enforcement agencies have the information they need to progress critical investigations. We will continue ongoing engagement with Overseas Territories on these issues.”

articles.content:
What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.

The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.

Two days of additional negotiations made it the longest talks in the summit's history.

The failure to reach a deal triggered criticism from prominent climate advocates, including former US Vice President Al Gore, who wrote it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".

BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

articles.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.description: Eleven people are dead in the attack on Dymer, with rescue efforts ongoing to find those still missing from the residential building.
articles.content:
Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say

ByHafsa Khalil and Jessica Lamb
  • Published
    22 November 2026
Updated 23 November 2026 05:33 GMT

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".

Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.

In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.

Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
articles.description: The prime minister of Australia, which co-hosted COP31, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
articles.content:
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

ByMark Poynting, Esme Stallard and Justin Rowlatt
BBC Climate and Science
  • Published
    22 November 2026
Updated 1 hour ago

Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".

"That is the reality," he said on Monday.

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

Climate advocates reacted with dismay at the failure of the talks.

Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".

The COP process was "in need of significant reform", Gore wrote on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."

"It's time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world," he added.

Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.

But following the weekend's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday.

The UN climate process has "suffered setbacks before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title: Fewer than half in UK will pay TV licence fee within a decade, report warns
articles.description: Analysis for thinktank points to cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on content in ‘spiral of decline’Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline”.
articles.content:
Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline”.

With senior BBC figures concerned about the accelerating fall in licence fee sales, the independent projections also warn that the proportion of households paying the levy will further decline to less than a third by 2037-38 should the government persist with the corporation’s current funding model.

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, is preparing to publish proposed changes to the licence fee that will force anyone who watches a streaming service to pay it. Currently, only people who watch live TV or the BBC’s iPlayer have to pay the fee.

Projections by the respected independent media consultancy Oliver & Ohlbaum Associates point to an “unsustainable” cycle of falling income leading to lower spending on strong content that attracts audiences.

They show the BBC’s licence fee income – paid by 77% of households last year – could be worth less than half its current level in real terms by 2037-38, the next point at which the broadcaster’s funding model is renegotiated.

The BBC’s own internal licence fee income modelling is also said to be bleak, with the corporation already making painful cuts to programmes and staff.

Nandy’s proposed new funding model, which could form part of the BBC’s next 10-year charter, is expected to be published before the end of the year.

Extending the licence fee to streamers would put the BBC on a more sustainable footing. However, it will be controversial with major streamers such as Netflix, Disney, Amazon and YouTube, as well as their subscribers.

Other more radical proposals, such as a household levy for the BBC, have already been ruled out by the Treasury as politically impossible.

Like all media companies, the BBC is facing a myriad of pressures. The costs of making television have hugely increased, while the arrival of streamers and digital platforms has transformed viewing habits.

Meanwhile, freezes to the licence fee over the past decade, as well as extra costs loaded on to the BBC by previous governments, have given the corporation less to spend.

The new independent projections, included in a report on the BBC by the Reset Tech thinktank, show why the broadcaster’s leadership and ministers accept that the status quo cannot continue.

The study suggests the BBC’s spending on TV content will more than halve by the next charter review. BBC viewing per person via TV sets would fall from 46 minutes a day in 2024-25 to just 23 minutes a day in 2037-38. Revenue would fall from £3.8bn to £1.6bn in real terms.

The BBC remains the UK’s most-used media brand, reaching 94% of adults every month. However, the projections suggest YouTube could overtake BBC TV set viewing in 2032-33.

It is predicted that more than half of households will not pay the licence fee by 2033-34. Non-payment of the licence fee has already risen from about 9% of households in 2015 to about 23% last year, and the trend has been accelerating.

Dylan Sparks, the UK director at Reset Tech, said the report confirmed that the BBC’s current funding model was broken. “The BBC is critical national infrastructure and it deserves a long-term settlement that ensures it not only survives but thrives in the decades to come,” he said.

“We urge the government to defend this vital British asset and to use the BBC charter renewal process to come forward with a new funding model that is universal, affordable and sustainable.”

A BBC spokesperson said: “We have consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform. We will continue to engage with government to secure a new charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come.”
articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor

articles.title: Love made a fool of Beau Lamarre-Condon but did not make him a murderer, defence argues
articles.description: Crown says accused former officer developed ‘jealous obsession’ but defence says ‘he was a poorly behaved boyfriend’Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastLove made a fool of Beau Lamarre-Condon, but it did not make him a
articles.content:
Love made a fool of Beau Lamarre-Condon, but it did not make him a murderer, his lawyer has told a court.

Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter, claiming the two men died while he acted in “self-defence”.

Lamarre-Condon developed a “jealous obsession” with Baird when the two were casually and non-exclusively dating in late 2022 and 2023, the prosecution argued.

The accused has admitted to going through Baird’s phone to delete and block other men, to entering the Paddington home one night and running off with Baird’s wallet and phone, and to watching Baird have sex with another man through his bedroom window.

But in his closing statement to the New South Wales supreme court, defence barrister John Stratton SC claimed this was because he had fallen “head over heels” in love with Baird and quoted English novelist William Thackeray.

“‘Love makes fools of us all,’ and you certainly might think that that very much applies to all of us whether young or old, straight or gay, male or female,” Stratton said.

“There’s no doubt the accused, Beau Lamarre-Condon, did plenty of foolish things and you might think the level of them was unusual, that he was a poorly behaved boyfriend.

“There’s a long distance between his admitting that sort of behaviour, and you finding him guilty of murder.”

But crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC urged the jury to reject Lamarre-Condon’s account and convict him on all three counts, as he finished his closing statement on Monday.

“The case is that the accused, driven by this jealous obsession, drove to Paddington in a hire car, scoped the house and waited for his opportunity,” he told the court.

Lamarre-Condon entered the house with a gun loaded with stolen bullets, and shot Baird in the back and temple, Hatfield alleged.

“It was not self-defence or an accident,” he said. “The evidence speaks only to an execution.”

Lamarre-Condon had testified he shot Baird after he lunged at him with a knife.

During this struggle, his gun was then flung across the room and picked up by Davies before the officer grabbed his arm and pushed the gun towards Davies.

Davies then pulled the trigger and shot himself, Lamarre-Condon told the court.

But this defence rests entirely on his own account and even if Baird had picked up a knife, it would not have assisted him against a Glock pistol, Hatfield said.

“You might think he is a proven and persistent liar and such a scenario is completely contrary to the weight of the evidence,” he told the court.

“The accused’s account is not the truth. It is a story made up after the fact in an attempt to meet the evidence.”

But Stratton said there were two serious problems with the crown case about Davies’ death that the prosecution “hasn’t overcome and can never overcome”.

Though Davies’ DNA was found on the trigger of the gun, there was no blood, the jury heard.

Davies being the source of the majority of DNA on this part of the gun is “powerful” evidence his finger was on the trigger when the third shot was fired, Stratton said.

The prosecution also failed to locate the bullet or any bullet fragments of the shot that struck Davies, and this is enough to leave jurors with reasonable doubt about the crown case, the barrister said.

“The forensic and ballistic evidence makes it more likely that the accused’s version is true, than the version the crown seeks to persuade,” he told the court.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
articles.author: Kat Wong

articles.title: ‘Difficult geopolitical times’: Albanese defends Bowen after Cop31 deal failure
articles.description: Coalition calls for climate change minister to resign immediately or be sacked over ‘catastrophic diplomatic disaster’, despite offering no alternatives on reducing emissionsSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereAnthony Albanese has defended Chris Bow
articles.content:
Anthony Albanese has defended Chris Bowen from criticism following the failure of the UN Cop31 climate summit, blaming the result on “difficult geopolitical times” as the Coalition called for the minister to resign.

Bowen served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, helping run the conference with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum.

Speaking to journalists late on Sunday after a list of countries rejected a proposed “cover decision” – an overarching agreement – for the conference, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the “red lines” he and his staff tried to negotiate to find consensus between nearly 200 countries were unbridgeable.

The biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize told the conference they would not accept a deal without it.

Saudi Arabia and Russia led a group of oil-rich countries that vowed to veto a decision that included mention of fossil fuels.

Bowen told reporters: “I would have been happy with [a] transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support.”

He said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and happening at speed. He said more than 90 countries had signed a pledge to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 – a step that should help cut fossil fuel use if delivered – but acknowledged the result was “very disappointing”.

Australia was sharply criticised during the conference for its continued support for new coal and gas export developments. Speaking on Monday, Albanese said Australia’s efforts had been critical in building relationships with Pacific neighbours.

“It’s evidence that we’re living in difficult geopolitical times,” he said of the result. “That is the reality. The important work of Cop is the work that we’ve done with the Pacific, where Australia and our Pacific leaders have worked constructively together.

“In order to have credibility [in the Pacific], the entry fee is action on climate change.”

The Coalition’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said Bowen should “resign immediately”.

“If Chris Bowen does not resign immediately, the prime minister should sack him,” Tehan said. “As the lead negotiator, Chris Bowen is personally responsible for this catastrophic diplomatic disaster.”

The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it was a “disastrous embarrassment” that Australia had chaired negotiations over the failed deal. In a statement, she said Labor was “not fit to lead – not on the world stage for climate negotiations, and not at home when it comes to protecting Australians from climate destruction”.

The Coalition, and Tehan specifically, have consistently attacked Labor’s bid to host the conference and Bowen’s installation as president of negotiations. Bowen argued for the role – newly created for Cop31 – after Turkey won the hosting rights after a protracted stand0ff.

Tehan did not say what the Coalition would have done differently if he was in Bowen’s shoes, other than saying the opposition would not have pursued hosting Cop or the position of president of negotiations. The Coalition has abandoned its support for Australia reaching net zero emissions by 2050 – a target introduced under former Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison – and promised to abolish Labor’s climate policies if elected.

It has not put forward any policies to reduce emissions.

Tehan said the consensus model of agreement used at the UN summit was “completely and utterly broken”. “Chris Bowen should have known that,” he said.

While the failure to get countries to agree to the “Antalya pact” in Turkey was a significant moment in the history of UN climate summits, the talks did not collapse completely.

The sticking point was the attempt to find language to reflect the “transition away for fossil fuels” that had been agreed to in 2023 in Dubai.

In the final stages of the talks, countries were presented with a text that only referred back to that decision and did not explicitly say “fossil fuels” – infuriating a sweep of countries.

Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a Cop veteran, said the lack of agreement on the main document at Cop31 – there was consensus on some minor issues – should not be seen as a failure of the entire Cop process but as “a successful defence of the [UN climate convention’s] integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels”.

Amanda Cahill, founder of the Next Economy, was in Antalya to offer advice on elements of the conference dealing with the so-called “just transition” – a wide-reaching set of guidelines meant to protect communities and workers affected by climate change and the shift away from the fossil fuel industry.

“While we didn’t get the outcome we wanted at this Cop, we maintained the global commitment to justice and equity as countries transition their economies to deal with climate change,” she said.

“We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us, but parties have committed to ensuring the Just Transition Mechanism is set up and that countries can get the support they need to implement meaningful and just climate action.”

Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said countries had “understandably” rejected a pact that he said “failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them”.

“The prime minister’s snub of the UN secretary general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit,” he said.
articles.author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya and Josh Butler in Canberra

articles.title: Unemployment to surpass 5% and ‘things will get a bit harder’, treasurer Jim Chalmers warns
articles.description: Economists flag rising recession risk as government forecasts economy will grow by less than 2% in 2027 and 2028Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet our daily political email, free app or daily news podcastJim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harde
articles.content:
Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget update will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.

As economists flagged rising recessionary risks, the treasurer used a ministerial statement during question time to reveal what he described as “concerning” economic numbers in the upcoming mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

Alongside higher unemployment, high fuel costs meant inflation would slow from 4.7% now to only “the mid-3s” by the middle of next year – or about 1 percentage point higher than anticipated in the May budget.

The economy was now expected to grow by less than 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

“We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier,” Chalmers told parliament.

“If Treasury was updating the mid-year forecasts today, they would reflect this difficult environment we’re in. In the near term, they’d forecast softer growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment.”

With a majority of Australians blaming public spending for driving this year’s inflation outbreak, Chalmers promised that the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include “net savings” to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“It’s not a mini-budget full of new initiatives but it will have some budget-sized savings. At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on,” he said.

News last week that the unemployment rate had climbed to 4.9% in October has turbocharged fears that a series of Reserve Bank interest rate hikes are weighing more heavily than anticipated – and that the economy could even tip into a deeper downturn next year.

Chalmers said the government’s short-term goal was “cutting spending enough, without threatening growth” – an approach he described as “a delicate balance”.

“We know that no realistic amount of savings makes inflation go away, but too much new spending can make it worse,” he said.

With the full effect of the five rate hikes only likely to become apparent through 2027, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, predicted economic growth would slump from 2.3%, to below 1%.

“We could flirt with recession next year,” Oliver said, putting the chances of a more severe downturn at a “high and rising” 40%.

Official figures on Wednesday are likely to show inflation climbing to nearly 5%, and Oliver agreed with the treasurer that getting the settings right in the mid-year budget would be “a difficult balancing act”.

“The government has been copping political blame for inflation, and Chalmers is under a lot of pressure to cut [spending]; but if he cuts too much it could accentuate the recession risks.”

The treasurer foreshadowed that any new spending decisions – such as Monday’s announcement that the $25 price cap on prescription medicine would be extended until the end of the decade at a cost of $242m – would be more than offset by savings measures.

But he also flagged that the mix of a weaker economy and “big unavoidable spending commitments” meant bigger deficits in the later years of the forward estimates period.

“It would not be responsible to fully offset these big changes to revenue and payments that flow through automatically from weaker economic parameters,” he argued.
articles.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor

articles.title: Doula thought self-described birth keeper was clinically trained before NSW baby death, inquest hears
articles.description: Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears doula urged client to attend birth centreFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastA doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals p
articles.content:
A doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals present has told an inquest that she thought a self-described birth keeper who was assisting her was clinically trained.

The child, known in court as Baby R, died after the free birth. Baby R’s death is one of four being examined in a joint coronial inquest in Lismore, which has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024.

Sita Tara Kali, a doula who was expected to give evidence later on Monday, was involved in the care of two of the four babies – including Baby R, who is thought to have died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth.

On Monday morning, another doula present for Baby R’s birth, Ione Maslin, gave evidence at the inquest.

Maslin told the inquest that she was not medically trained, and had attended about 30 to 40 births before Baby R’s death. She said that Baby R’s birth was the first she had attended without a midwife present.

She told the inquest she now wouldn’t feel comfortable supporting a birth without a midwife present because “doulas need to be working together with the healthcare system”.

The inquest heard that the baby’s mother had hoped that the Byron Bay Birth Centre would be able to provide her with a midwife, but that the she was told she lived too far away.

“She started looking for a private midwife but still she maintained the hope that the hospital would be able to provide her with care,” Maslin, who is from Brazil, told the inquest through a Portuguese translator.

“I insisted for her to go to the birth centre to have the baby … I suggested her to go and visit and feel the energy and to know that it was OK and safe.”

The inquest last week heard that Baby R’s mother had a general distrust of hospitals and felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to her baby.

Maslin told the inquest that Kali had come on as a second doula during the pregnancy. She said she was under the impression that Kali was clinically trained, but was “not a registered professional”.

The inquest last week heard that, at 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that Baby R was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent, and the mother was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth.

The woman contacted Kali, the inquest heard, who said in a police statement that “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. ‘Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do’.”

Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. He was white in colour and never latched on to feed, the inquest heard.

About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The court heard that Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

The inquest continues.
articles.author: Jordyn Beazley
