Transcript Audio

In a lengthy press conference, President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia and defended his relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. White House correspondent Liz Landers was in the briefing room as the president took questions from reporters.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

In a lengthy press conference today, President Donald Trump touted his recent trip to Asia and defended his relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, was in the Briefing Room today as the president took questions from reporters. She joins me now.

So, Liz, let's begin with that trilateral meeting in China the president just returned from. What did he have to say about that today?

Liz Landers:

Well, he just got back from Shenzhen late last night. He gave a glowing review of this trip that he took, in particular, that trilateral meeting between Russia, the U.S., and China.

And he defended calling President Putin a friend. He was asked today, whether Putin is a friend of America, and he wouldn't really answer that part, saying, I don't know if he's a friend of the U.S., but said that we, Donald Trump and Putin, have a fantastic relationship.

Secretary Rubio was also at the podium there today, and took some questions from reporters, and sort of defended what the president was talking about with this visit. Here's what he said.

Marco Rubio:

These three countries, the United States, Russia, and China, between these three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet.

The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd. It's dangerous. And if these leaders can't get along and can't engage with one another and don't have a positive relationship, it is impossible to get anything good done for the country and the safety of the world.

Liz Landers:

So, Rubio there kind of prebutting some of this criticism or responding to some of this criticism that we have heard in Washington, in particular from Democrats, saying, why did President Trump invite Putin to this meeting and elevate Russia, which has a much smaller economy than the U.S. and China, and also is in the middle of this war with Ukraine?

Another point that I just wanted to make, Amna, President Trump keeps saying that President Putin wants peace. He said that again today. But President Putin and Russia bombed Ukraine just this morning.

Amna Nawaz:

Meanwhile, the president also made some news when it comes to regulating AI data centers. What should we understand about that?

Liz Landers:

Yes, the president has been an ardent defender of data centers really since this has become a burgeoning policy and politics issue. Especially, it was in the midterms too. We heard that from voters. He made this announcement earlier today.

President Donald Trump:

We're not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it. We want them to build it here.

Liz Landers:

The president has said repeatedly that many cities and states want to have these data centers, that they are a -- quote -- "tremendous asset." That was something that he reiterated again today.

And he said that the U.S. needs to have these centers, these data centers here, to be competitive with China in this AI race. These data centers are a physical aspect of this race with AI, and he said that he wants them here instead of China.

One of the things that I think came up today as well throughout this briefing, were questions that he was not really answering about Jensen Huang. And since this news has come out that he stepped down from Nvidia earlier this week, the administration has tried to be more aggressive about AI chips and regulation, and they put out this new policy on Monday clamping down on who can export chips across the world.

Amna Nawaz:

Meanwhile, Liz, as we have been reporting, the White House is also preparing for this change in Congress, right? In just a few short months, the president's going to have to work with Democratic majorities in both the House and the Senate.

How did he address that today?

Liz Landers:

The president vacillates between saying that he wants to veto anything that comes across his desk, and then says that he wants to work with Democrats.

Today, he said that he thinks that the incoming likely speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, is smart and that, if Democrats want to work with him, then he will be willing to do that. There were two areas, though, in particular, that he identified that he thinks there's some bipartisanship, health care and also immigration. He did not get into specifics on those policies at all.

Amna Nawaz:

We will wait and see.

White House correspondent Liz Landers beginning our coverage.

Liz, thank you.

Liz Landers:

Of course.

In our news wrap Friday, stocks tumbled to end the week as worries about AI rattled the market, a second federal judge is blocking President Trump's triumphal arch in Washington and a federal appeals court is blocking the Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

We start the day's other headlines on Wall Street, where stocks tumbled to end the week, as worries about AI rattled the market.

(BELL RINGING)

Amna Nawaz:

By the closing bell, all three major averages were deeply in the red, as investors weigh the health of the AI sector following Nvidia's leadership upheaval and Anthropic's record IPO.

Looking at the numbers, the Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 900 points on the day. The Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent, erasing all its gains for the year. The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, meaning it's now in what investors call correction territory.

A second federal judge is blocking President Trump's Memorial Arch in Washington, D.C. The judge in Virginia called the project a rush job today, saying it lacks a legal basis. She put construction there on hold indefinitely, pending the outcome of legal challenges to the arch.

Earlier this week, a separate judge extended a previous block for two more weeks. President Trump is trying to build a 250-foot Memorial Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, which has led to criticism from veterans groups and local environmentalists.

In Iowa, a federal appeals court is blocking the U.S. Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks. The controlled explosion has been scheduled for today, and was expected to send lead dust as far as 60 miles around the area.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had agreed to postpone the detonation until Monday. But he warned that a coming drop in temperatures could further destabilize the material. It's unclear whether the court will weigh in again before Monday.

In Florida, heavy storms are moving north after drenching parts of the Atlantic coast. Torrential rains turned roads into waterways, with some areas already seeing their wettest November on record. The National Hurricane Center is warning of severe widespread flash flooding for parts of Eastern Florida and says the threat could carry into next week.

In the meantime, across the country, in California, heavy flooding left some neighborhoods in Los Angeles underwater, as surging waters affected a large stretch of the California coast.

In Poland, authorities say two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in Polish territory overnight. In Southeastern Poland, CCTV footage showed a large explosion and a bright flash. The crash site was around 20 miles from where European troops from 11 countries were taking part in rare military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar Ukraine mission.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursions an intentional provocation and said Poland, which neighbors both Ukraine and Russia must be involved in future peace talks.

Donald Tusk (through interpreter):

It seems that we are dealing with an intentional provocation. It is no coincidence that these objects fell near the site where military exercises are taking place. I will always act with great prudence. No one wants the situation to escalate or worsen.

Amna Nawaz:

Meantime, Russia carried out news strikes on Ukraine overnight and into today as part of its response to Kyiv's recent attacks on a strategic bridge. Authorities in Western Ukraine said a Russian attack on a railway station killed at least two people. And officials in the Southeast say a Russian-guided bomb hit a residential area, injuring at least four people, including a child.

The U.K. and the European Union agreed to a series of deals today, as the two sides seek closer ties a decade after Britain voted to leave the bloc, also known as Brexit. The agreement would relax restrictions on agricultural trade, cut carbon taxes on some exports, and allow 100,000 young people to live and work in each other's countries.

Today's summit in Brussels did not resolve questions about university fees and the broader post-Brexit relationship. But European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the deal a turning point, while Britain's prime minister described this as a historic moment.

Andy Burnham, British Prime Minister:

This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe. Britain in 2026 is in a different place, but so is Europe. And people look at the world and they would think people of like mind need to work together. They need to get closer.

Amna Nawaz:

The U.K. formally exited the E.U. in 2020 after nearly half-a-century of membership. Polling suggests that most British voters are now in favor of closer ties with Europe amid a sluggish economy and growing global tensions.

Well, a spacecraft is about to enter orbit around Mercury for only the second time in history. The BepiColombo mission is a joint European and Japanese effort. It launched eight years ago and traveled roughly six billion miles to reach the planet closest to the sun. The probe will split in two to map the planet's surface and interior.

Researchers are hoping for clues into how mercury formed and how ice and other materials have survived on its surface, among other questions. NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft was the first to orbit Mercury, collecting data between 2011 and 2015.

And Rockstar Games says "Grand Theft Auto VI" set a record with nearly $3.8 billion in global sales in just its first day. Rockstar also says it sold more than 32 million units in presales, another record. The standard edition of the open-world crime series retails for roughly $80 in the U.S. It's the first franchise release in 13 years.

For context, that one-day total is about a billion dollars more than the top-grossing film of all time, "Avengers: Endgame," made during its entire worldwide run in theaters.

articles.content:
Thom Tillis move comes after Michael LoSapio, nominated for Cisa role, told hearing ‘I don’t believe it was an attack’

Senator Thom Tillis, the outgoing North Carolina Republican who is due to be replaced by a Democrat, has reportedly blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead a key US cybersecurity agency, Michael LoSapio, after he denied during a hearing that the Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.

Tillis, who declined to run for re-election and after repeated clashes with Trump’s, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination to serve as a director of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (Cisa). His block on the nomination will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.

articles.description: President Trump has replaced the nation's top cybersecurity official following a string of seemingly unrelated technology outages over the last couple of weeks. Officials have repeatedly stressed that these outages were not the result of intentional attacks, but given the growth of AI, there's growi
articles.content:
By —

William Brangham William Brangham

By —

Karina Cuevas Karina Cuevas

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/mounting-tech-disruptions-raise-concerns-about-u-s-cybersecurity
  • Email

Transcript Audio

President Trump has replaced the nation’s top cybersecurity official following a string of seemingly unrelated technology outages over the last couple of weeks. Officials have repeatedly stressed that these outages were not the result of intentional attacks, but given the growth of AI, there’s growing concern that attacks are on the horizon. William Brangham discussed more with Chris Krebs.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

President Trump has replaced the nation's top cybersecurity official following a string of seemingly unrelated technology outages over the last couple of weeks. Those outages raise serious concerns about the stability of crucial digital systems.

William Brangham has more.

William Brangham:

Amna, these disruptions, which happened across major computer networks, demonstrate how a single failure can affect critical systems used by millions of Americans.

In just a matter of days, outages have affected Microsoft, which left millions of users without e-mail access, the FAA, which triggered a nationwide flight stoppage for several hours, major U.S. banks, like J.P. Morgan Chase, which temporarily snarled customer transactions, and the National Security Agency, where its internal communication network was interrupted.

Officials have repeatedly stressed that these outages were not the result of intentional attacks, but, given the growth of artificial intelligence and its ability to identify vulnerabilities in our software, there's growing concern that attacks are on the horizon.

For more on this, we are joined again by Chris Krebs. He's the founder of The Krebs Group and used to be the nation's top cybersecurity official during the first Trump administration.

Chris, great to have you back on the program.

Christopher Krebs, Former Director, U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency: Thanks for having me.

William Brangham:

Before we get to this new cybersecurity official that the president has announced, let's talk about these outages.

As I mentioned, officials keep saying these are not attacks, these are patches being done to fix glitches that have been discovered in the system. What do you make of that analysis?

Christopher Krebs:

I think it's spot on, based on my conversations with folks in some of the affected organizations. Yes, there were patches. There were bugs that were discovered in software that were subsequently fixed.

What's happening in the background, though, I think is the real story. Since April of 2026, when Anthropic released Mythos preview, which is an AI frontier model, which means it's the best of the best -- it was trained specifically for cybersecurity research.

And basically what you have is an amalgamation of every hacker, every security researcher that's ever existed on the face of the Earth that will work tirelessly on its goal. It doesn't sleep, it doesn't eat, it doesn't need a coffee break.

And those models have been used by the good guys, by companies like Microsoft, by companies like IBM and Google. And they are looking at their code that exists today, and they're trying to find as many bugs as fast as they can before the bad guys that are also using AI, not as good as these frontier models, but nonetheless they have AI, and trying to get those patched.

And, in part, what's happened over the last several days is these companies that are patching their systems to get -- to hide these bugs to get rid of these bugs, they're doing it in a way that's very fast, but it's also stacking up a number of bugs or patches for those bugs.

And any time you patch a system, you introduce a nonzero chance of destabilizing that network. And, unfortunately, that's what happened this week. But, again, they were all outages that were brief, they were blips. If this was a real cyberattack, you would either see those systems never recovering or taking days, if not weeks, to get back up and running.

William Brangham:

So, if these are just patches, as you said, and, in a sense, benign, that these are attempts to put Band-Aids on little wounds that are being found, it still does demonstrate the fragility, it seems, of so many systems that undergird our entire society.

Christopher Krebs:

A thousand percent. And it's more than that.

It shows how much of our daily lives today is driven by technology, is connected. And that's only going to increase going forward. I don't know what five years down the road looks like, but I will tell you that more things are going to be connected, more things are going to rely on digital technology.

What we have to do is keep using AI. The good guys have to keep using AI to find as many of those bugs as possible, patch them, fix them before the bad guys do. Do I know how long that's going to take? No. And anybody that says they know, I don't think they're telling the truth.

But this could be a extended period of time. And I'm not talking just a couple months. Could be a year or more until we root out all these bugs, patch them, and make sure the Internet's a safer place. I do think that there's a silver lining to all of this.

William Brangham:

Don't you fear someday, though, that this AI arms race, that the bad guys, as you call them, have tools that are equivalent to the good guys, and that we do start to see it used not as a detective tool, but as an offensive tool?

Christopher Krebs:

It is already today being used as an offensive tool.

Over the last couple of weeks, a number of organizations have been hit by what's known as an agentic offensive framework, known as ARTEX. There are a couple others, but basically it's software harness that sits on top of models, like some of the open-source models we have here, or DeepSeek and Kimi and GLM that are Chinese open-source models.

And like I said, they're being pointed at systems. They're scanning, doing recon on a network on a company. They're looking for vulnerabilities, and they never stop. Time used to be in the defenders' advantage. Now time doesn't matter. These bad guys are using it, and they're going all the time.

William Brangham:

President Trump, as we mentioned, has announced a new director of cybersecurity, the job that you used to have.

Kirsten Davies, she used to have this job at the Pentagon. She is now going to be the new head of cybersecurity in the U.S. What do you make of her appointment and what do you think she ought to be focusing on day one?

Christopher Krebs:

Well, to separate it out, there's the job, the Office of the National Cyber Director at the White House. That's a more recently created position. And there's a job that I had, which was the director of the CISA, the agency.

Both had important personnel activities this week. But Sean Cairncross, the prior Office of National Cyber Director, the director, was relieved of his duties yesterday. And, as you mentioned, Kirsten Davies came in.

The president today in a press conference said that he didn't think Sean was doing a particularly good job, so he replaced him. Look, anyway, you cut it, Kirsten is a competent technologist. She's in the job.

She is very likely focusing on the -- just what we're talking about today, the outages, but also working with the nation's critical infrastructure providers and the AI labs to find as many vulnerabilities in our most critical systems, get them patched up, and make sure that things are safe, safe and secure.

William Brangham:

Not an ideal -- it's a tough job to have right now.

Chris Krebs of The Krebs Group, great to see you. Thanks.

Christopher Krebs:

Thanks so much.

articles.description: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is fresh off a reelection campaign that gave him another four years in office and Democrats majorities in the state House. Now Shapiro is turning his attention to foreign policy, laying out his prescriptions to solve pressing global crises. Amna Nawaz sat down with the
articles.content:
By —

Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz

By —

Matt Loffman Matt Loffman

By —

Doug Adams Doug Adams

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/josh-shapiro-on-foreign-policy-democratic-wins-and-his-2028-ambitions
  • Email
  • Facebook

  • Tumblr
Share on Facebook Share on Twitter
Transcript Audio

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is fresh off a reelection campaign that gave him another four years in office and Democrats majorities in the state House. Now Shapiro is turning his attention to foreign policy, laying out his prescriptions to solve pressing global crises. Amna Nawaz sat down with the governor to discuss his vision for how the United States should engage on the world stage.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro is fresh off a reelection campaign that gave him another four years in office, and Democrats majorities in the Statehouse and in Washington.

Now Shapiro, among the many potential candidates eying higher office in 2028, is turning his attention to foreign policy, laying out his prescriptions to solve some pressing global crises in a speech at the University of Pennsylvania today.

I sat down with the governor at Perry World House to discuss his vision for how the United States should engage on the world stage.

Governor Shapiro, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us.

Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA):

Great to be with you. Thank you.

Amna Nawaz:

So I got to ask you, what's the governor of Pennsylvania doing delivering a speech on foreign policy if he's not running for president?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

I must tell you that it matters to governors what is happening across the globe. It matters that we have stability across the globe to get investment in our states.

It matters for the citizens that we represent. And I spoke about that today, the importance of strengthening both security and prosperity and the benefit it could have for the people of Pennsylvania.

Amna Nawaz:

I want to ask you about news this week, because you said in your speech: "The chaos, the cruelty, the corruption of this administration has made the U.S. less secure at home and abroad."

We just saw the president lead this sort of historic trilateral meeting. You have got the president of China there, the president of Russia. This administration would argue, you have to meet with these kinds of leaders, that that kind of meeting actually makes America more safe.

You could potentially work to end the war in Ukraine. You could strike some kind of nuclear arms deal. Do you agree those meetings are necessary by world leaders?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Well, it's one thing to have dialogue. I'm not arguing with having dialogue.

But I thought what the president did was, he showed himself to be profoundly and pathetically weak on the international stage. You mentioned in your question that you have to dialogue to address Ukraine or address other issues. Absolutely.

The problem is, the president didn't address it, didn't address AI, didn't push back on the Russians and their aggressions toward Ukraine, didn't do anything to push back on the work that China is doing to undermine our economy. None of that. He just enjoyed the pageantry.

And I actually thought that he ended up looking like the junior partner on the international stage.

Amna Nawaz:

What do you mean by that?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

We are being led around by a weak individual, who is bringing chaos to the global stage.

I thought, in particular, when the three of them, Putin, Xi, and Trump, were walking together, it was clear that Xi was dominating that scene.

Amna Nawaz:

At the center of the three of them.

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

And Trump looked incredibly small.

Amna Nawaz:

On the war in Iran, you also mentioned in your speech that you think these midterm wins for Democrats give you an opportunity to develop a new foreign policy. You say you want Democrats to use their new majorities to try to end this Iran war.

What does that specifically look like? What kind of legislation can they be passing, especially when they don't have a veto-proof majority?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Well, they have a war powers resolution and they got the power of the purse. And they've got to use their leverage to end this war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

I have confidence in the speaker-designate and his majority in the House and the new majority in the Senate to do what is necessary to use their leverage to stop this war, this war that is creating chaos overseas and in the Arab world, and a war that is driving up prices for people here at home.

Amna Nawaz:

There's another big issue that continues to really divide members of your party, in particular, and that is the U.S. approach and support for the state of Israel.

You saw earlier this year a number of Senate Democrats, including many folks who are sort of eying a 2028 run, voting to block some arms sales to Israel. Would you support efforts like that? And would you have voted with them?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Look, I think, in many ways, this issue is being resolved.

You saw before that the president and the current prime minister in Israel have indicated that they are planning to end the military aid that's existed for decades to Israel. I support that. I think it is important to end that military aid.

I do think it is important for Israel to be able to have the weapons they need to defend themselves from attacks from terrorist organizations, be it Hamas, the Houthis, the Iranians. And why do I think that? Because it's in America's national security interest.

Amna Nawaz:

You mentioned in your remarks sort of tying together America's economic future and its national security future, the message that needs to be delivered to allies.

You specifically mentioned as well even Canada signing a new deal with China. We've seen this with a number of our allies working around or without the U.S.

What kind of message can you deliver to allies to convince them that this is a long-term relationship that they can rely on if they're believing that every four years with a new administration policies could shift?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Look, I meet regularly with foreign leaders, ambassadors, foreign ministers, in some cases prime ministers.

And I want them to understand that there are other voices in America that believe in alliances, other governors who believe that, other members of Congress who believe that. It is not just the approach of the president that I think reflects the will of the American people.

In fact, I don't think that he reflects where we are. I think America believes in alliances, but we have to make sure those alliances pay off for the American people from a prosperity perspective and from a defense perspective and a security perspective.

Amna Nawaz:

If I may, though, it's the president and his administration that sets that foreign policy, right? That's what allies have to trust.

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

And I think he is setting it poorly. You asked about the future. And I spoke about this earlier.

I don't think it will be enough for the next American president, for the next group of members of Congress, or even the next group of governors to simply stand up, as Joe Biden did when he took over as president -- I think I'm paraphrasing now -- where he said America's back or something to that effect.

I don't think words will cut it anymore. The destruction that Trump has done I think is going to take maybe generations to be able to repair.

Amna Nawaz:

We're just coming off these historic Democratic wins in the midterm elections, the blue wave, the blue tsunami, whatever you want to call it. Your reelection win in particular was even bigger than your last by 22 points.

But we also saw Democrats win statewide in places like Kansas and Mississippi and South Carolina and the Senate races on that front. How much of your win do you believe was because of you, because of Josh Shapiro, and how much was part of this blue wave?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Well, it was obviously a great night for Democrats and a complete rejection, not just of Donald Trump, but his enablers.

Look, you can be the pundit and decide what my election means. I could tell you that Pennsylvania is the swingiest swing state in the country. I mean, Donald Trump has won it two of the last three times. I've now set a record every election I've run in and just set another one.

Amna Nawaz:

I know you like to talk about getting stuff done, that GSD.

(CROSSTALK)

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

It's PBS, so we'll say stuff, yes.

(LAUGHTER)

Amna Nawaz:

You also now have the first Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania in three decades. So what is your single biggest priority that you know you need to push through early to try to make sure that everyone who swung your way in this election doesn't swing back the other in the next two years?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Well, we have a long agenda that we will carry out first over the first 100 days and then over the course of the next two years.

But the first bill that will reach my desk in January will be to raise our minimum wage from a paltry $7.25 an hour to at least 15 bucks an hour.

Amna Nawaz:

That's your single biggest priority right now?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Well, that will be the first bill that reaches my desk.

Amna Nawaz:

I want to ask you about a health issue I know we've been struggling with here in Pennsylvania, and that is the measles outbreaks.

We saw the Pan American Health Organization say the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status because of the country's inability to control those outbreaks. Pennsylvania has been ground zero for those. You've got some 1,529 cases reported in this year. That's more than double any other state.

What more as governor can you be doing to mitigate that?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Yes, and, sadly, if I can add to that, eight deaths as well, so eight families here in Pennsylvania without a loved one because of a disease that was eliminated 26 years ago in America, and now it has come roaring back.

It's come roaring back because of vaccine misinformation and disinformation, because we know -- don't take my word for it. The medical experts have shown, the data bears out that the MMR -- that's the measles vaccine -- is your best protection against measles, particularly the kind of measles that will really sicken you and claim your life.

But grifters like RFK have spent now a generation, and now over the last two years as the health secretary, undermining people's confidence in medicine, undermining their confidence in vaccines. And you can draw a straight line between that work enabled by this president, promoted by this president, and the number of people getting sick across the country and the fact that we have lost our designation now, designation of eliminating measles.

You ask, what can we do about it? The good news is, the people of Pennsylvania are doing what we do best. We are coming together to attack this problem.

Amna Nawaz:

I know you have been asked multiple times, and you have not been yet ready to say if you will or won't run for president in 2028. But you have said that you want to be part of that conversation in 2028. I guess, what would make you decide not to run at this point? What kind of questions are you asking yourself?

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

I want to make sure that, as the governor of Pennsylvania, that my voice is helping shape not just the future of our party, but hopefully the future direction of our country that doesn't include Donald Trump and his enablers.

As for what I might do professionally in the future, that's a personal decision that my wife, our four kids, and I will make at some point soon here. But it is -- my focus is on the work. My focus is on getting out what my views are that I think can help promote security and stability at home and abroad.

And I'm going to continue to lift up my voice as the governor of Pennsylvania in that conversation.

Amna Nawaz:

That's the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro, joining us today.

Governor, thank you for your time.

Gov. Josh Shapiro:

Thank you. Thanks for being here.

articles.title: Fiona's caretakers and fans mourn the beloved hippo after her death at Cincinnati Zoo
articles.description: Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many.
articles.content:
By —

Obed Lamy, Associated Press Obed Lamy, Associated Press

By —

John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fionas-caretakers-and-fans-mourn-the-beloved-hippo-after-her-death-at-cincinnati-zoo

Fiona's caretakers and fans mourn the beloved hippo after her death at Cincinnati Zoo

Nation Nov 20, 2026 6:39 PM EST

CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday.

Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.

READ MORE: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, more than a week after ingesting a hat

The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.

Since her death, Fiona's fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats.

"She brought so much love in her lifetime," said one note.

Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.

During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for "anyone that was going through hard times."

Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years.

"The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles."

Fiona makes her debut to the media in Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo in Cincinnati, Ohio, May 2017. File photo by Liz Dufour/USA TODAY Network via Imagn Images via Reuters

One of Fiona's keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member.

"It has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire," Wingate wrote. "We lost her in the most horrific and tragic way."

She ended: "She was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry."

Fiona wasn't the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object.

In 1923, a hippo "came to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth," according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippo's remains from the Cincinnati Zoo. A taxidermist created a lifelike mold of the original specimen, but it's no longer part of the collection.

The zoo's team couldn't reach the hat in Fiona

Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona's digestive system wasn't meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said.

Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through.

Blood work showed her health was failing Thursday, so the zoo's animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippo's anatomy, he added.

Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he said.

The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines.

"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Jenike called the zoo's staff heroic in their efforts to save her.

Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona

At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.

But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.

The zoo's animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.

Fiona is mourned by many worldwide

Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries.

Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.

Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure "the smiles she gave me."

Fiona wasn't expected to survive her first weeks

Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.

The zoo's staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn't nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.

She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.

Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

Associated Press writer Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Brooks and Capehart on Trump's summit with Putin and Xi
articles.description: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including President Trump's trilateral summit with Xi and Putin, the ongoing debate surrounding data centers, and Elon Musk's attempt to distance himself from MAGA.
articles.content:
By —

Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz

By —

Jonah Anderson Jonah Anderson

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/brooks-and-capehart-on-trumps-summit-with-putin-and-xi
  • Email
  • Facebook
  • Twitter
  • LinkedIn
  • Pinterest
  • Tumblr
Share on Facebook Share on Twitter
Transcript Audio

David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including President Trump's trilateral summit with Xi and Putin, the ongoing debate surrounding data centers, and Elon Musk's attempt to distance himself from MAGA.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

Now, after a busy news week, we turn, as we do every Friday, to the analysis of Brooks and Jonathan. That's "The Atlantic's" David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW.

Great to see you both.

Jonathan Capehart:

Hey, Amna.

David Brooks:

Hi.

Amna Nawaz:

Let's start with the president, this trip overseas to China, the trilateral meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. You heard Governor Shapiro there say that the president looked weak. He said that U.S. interests were not advanced in these meetings.

David, you also heard him reference specifically images in which the president was walking with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and it was Xi Jinping in the middle, President Trump to the side as they all stood together and walked together. What was achieved in this meeting?

David Brooks:

Did FDR always sit in the middle and try -- when he was with Churchill and Stalin? I don't know -- think it matters who sits where.

You know, I interviewed an eminent historian yesterday named Arne Westad for my important podcast "The Permanent Questions."

(LAUGHTER)

David Brooks:

And he's worried that we're on the verge of a global war. And his argument is that world affairs becomes most dangerous when you have one rising power, China, and one relatively declining power. That's us.

And when that happens, as it happened before World War I, when you had a rising Germany and a declining Britain, is that the power dynamics of the world are scrambled. Nobody knows where they stand. Everybody feels insecure. You get these combinations of hubris and fear and anxiety, and people -- and they get rising nationalisms.

And people do crazy stuff because they're just terrified of what the world has come to. And his argument is that the world is now -- with Xi and Putin and Trump, we're in that kind of world. And so that he thinks there's a possibility something like Sarajevo, some assassination, some crazy thing will happen, and everything will just go ballistic.

So having had that conversation with Arne, and then seeing this, I think nothing was advanced in the summit, but I can't be upset that the three leaders are meeting, because one of the things you do not want in a volatile world is people misinterpreting each other. You don't want them judging each other by their public statements.

You want them judging each other by the private statements that they say to each other, and that has a pacifying effect. And so I don't love the fact that Trump thinks Putin is a friend or that Xi is a friend. I don't think they're friends. But in -- with this alarming thing in my mind, I think, OK, at least they got together.

Amna Nawaz:

So, Jonathan, whether it's to mitigate a world war by meeting, or, as the president said, look, you have to engage even with your adversaries, what do you make of that?

Jonathan Capehart:

Yes, you should meet with your adversaries. President Trump is not the first American president to meet with America's adversaries.

What puts President Trump in a league of his own, one is that he believes that the leaders of Russia and China are his friends. Two, he went to the table to talk to them with no real agenda that is sort of an America-first agenda. And, three, he did not come away from the table with any deliverables.

You have a war in Ukraine that President Putin is waging, and you have got the United States at war with Iran, that China is helping Iran. Both of them are helping Iran. President Trump should have been at that table pounding his fists, saying to them, you guys have to cut out what you're doing, because, at a minimum, you are putting my service members at risk.

None of that happened. And the press conference today was enraging, because the president, the first thing he says is nothing about this -- nothing about the summit, nothing about any deliverables or tangible achievements.

It was about that plane that he got from Qatar, a used plane, mind you, that he flew overseas, bragging about how it can go faster and go farther, which makes me wonder, has it been armed with all the things that made Air Force One, a flying fortress -- we still don't know if the president of the United States is flying around on an extremely vulnerable plane.

And, as you can tell, I'm still mad about that -- about that press conference.

Amna Nawaz:

Well, can I get David to respond briefly to what you just said there about sort of -- take away the fact that maybe there weren't hard deliverables, that it is good that world leaders meet.

The messaging from the president after the fact has been very much that this was a win for the U.S., that he is friends, personal friends, with Putin, maybe not friends with the U.S. What do you make of that?

David Brooks:

Yes, I think both what Jonathan and I said are true at different levels.

And so I'm talking about the global picture of a possible another World War I. Like, that's up here.

Amna Nawaz:

Yes.

David Brooks:

But in the immediate context of the next six months, the war in Iran, the war in Ukraine, these are pieces of that, and they have the potential, not as big as Taiwan, but they have the potential to be flash points to create that larger crisis.

And so I agree with what Jonathan said. We are not friends with Putin. We should make that clear we find him repugnant, and we find Xi kind of repugnant. And the problem with Xi is that they're not just a rising power. They're a rising power possibly on the verge of decline. Their growth rates are collapsing.

Their demographics are terrible. Their debt is terrible. Their government is getting more and more erratic. And the most dangerous part of what you get when you get these power transfers is when a regime decides we have got a window to act, and that window is closing. And so we better do something about Taiwan.

And did Trump talk about any of this? Does he have the global vision to think what the world situation is? Obviously not. But it doesn't hurt to at least have some communication, so they don't -- the misunderstandings of each other are not legion.

Amna Nawaz:

I want to get to something else you mentioned about the president talking about at that press conference today Liz Landers was reporting on earlier as well.

The president talked about his view for AI data centers, as he's long supported them and further building here in the U.S. But that talk today did come after, Jonathan, these sweeping Republican losses in the midterms. We know data centers were a real issue in many races. In the midterm exit polls that were conducted by SSRS, they found 76 percent of Trump voters opposed new data centers in their community.

To hear the president today talk about them in this way, what did -- what struck you about that?

Jonathan Capehart:

It's just further evidence to my mind he is out of touch.

We often joke that the president and his followers are on Earth 2. Only on Earth 2 could you have the president of the United States the day before the midterms go to the Reflecting Pool and wax poetic about pipes and algae.

Remember, this is -- President Trump also during the campaign said that people should get on board with data centers and AI. Otherwise, they're going to be -- they're going to be poor. So this was not surprising.

But coming after an election where the American people, right up to election, we don't like this, we don't like what it's doing to our communities, to our bottom lines when it comes to electricity costs, what it's doing to our livelihoods, and he couldn't care less. That's the thing that gets me.

Amna Nawaz:

David?

David Brooks:

I agree with Trump on this one and disagree with 76 percent of his voters. So, first...

Amna Nawaz:

OK, direct your e-mails to David@...

(LAUGHTER)

David Brooks:

Yes, first, what are the objections to data centers?

First the water usage. Data centers use less than 1 percent of U.S. water usage. You want to -- you're worried about water? Go to golf courses. That's a much bigger problem if you care about water concern.

Second, electricity, that is a more serious issue because they do use a lot of electricity. Nonetheless, they still -- the increased electricity demand less than 10 percent of the increased demand is because of data centers. You're worried about electricity usage and the rising rates? E.V.s, electric vehicles, use more electricity than data centers, industrial production vastly more.

And so these are issues involved in data centers that can be mitigated if there's intelligent management of the data centers and intelligent policies. Meanwhile, every industry that we have ever had in this country, whether it's farming, whether it's of cars, whether it's aviation, they use resources.

articles.title: Inside the museum preserving the story of JFK's assassination
articles.description: On November 22, 1963, President John F. Kennedy was killed while driving in a motorcade in downtown Dallas. As the story continues to be told and questioned, those memories are preserved and displayed at The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown visited the muse
articles.content:
By —

Jeffrey Brown Jeffrey Brown

By —

Anne Azzi Davenport Anne Azzi Davenport

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/inside-the-museum-preserving-the-story-of-jfks-assassination
  • Email

Share on Facebook Share on Twitter
Transcript Audio

On November 22, 1963, President John F. Kennedy was killed while driving in a motorcade in downtown Dallas. As the story continues to be told and questioned, those memories are preserved and displayed at The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown visited the museum for our arts and culture series, CANVAS.

Read the Full Transcript

Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors.

Amna Nawaz:

November 22, 1963, a date forever etched in American historical memory, when President John F. Kennedy was shot and killed in his motorcade crossing Dealey Plaza in downtown Dallas.

The story continues to be told and questioned. How those memories are preserved and displayed at the site itself is the subject of our report from senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown for our arts and culture series, Canvas.

Jeffrey Brown:

The setting is central to the experience, a former book depository in downtown Dallas, now the Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza.

Curatorial head Stephen Fagin …

Stephen Fagin:

I think our job is to provide our audiences with the tools to navigate this interpretive minefield of history and culture that is the life, death, and legacy of President Kennedy.

Jeffrey Brown:

The youthful president who inspired millions, the challenges at home and abroad he faced in his short time in office, and inevitably and here most hauntingly the assassination of John F. Kennedy from shots investigators determined were fired from the sixth floor of this building by Lee Harvey Oswald on November 22, 1963.

Museum CEO Nicola Longford …

Nicola Longford:

We presume that everybody has some idea of what happened here, and, actually, quite a lot of our younger generations have no idea what happened here. This is their entry point into this story of President Kennedy and his life and his death, and why are we still talking about it?

Donald Sutherland, Actor:

Well, that's a real question, isn't it? Why?

Jeffrey Brown:

It's a fascination, even obsession that's endured in popular culture with movies and novels.

Kevin Costner, Actor:

I never realized Kennedy was so dangerous to the establishment.

Jeffrey Brown:

In countless books examining the assassination, in the interest from people all over the world. You can see it in the memory books here, the different nationalities, the personal memories and connections, those who will never accept the official U.S. government determination.

Stephen Fagin:

Baby Boomers who have childhood memories of being in a classroom and their teacher or their principal telling them about the assassination, seeing an adult cry for the first time.

But for younger people, this is a murder mystery. This is a CSI crime scene.

Jeffrey Brown:

Conspiracy? Who did it? The museum carefully asks the questions that have never gone away.

Darwin Payne:

This is the imagined city desk.

Jeffrey Brown:

Yes.

One floor up, a special exhibition personalizes events in another way with a multimedia presentation following four local newspaper reporters who worked on the story in November 1963.

Darwin Payne:

This is the newsroom.

Jeffrey Brown:

Including now 89-year-old Darwin Payne, then 26 and on the rewrite desk at the now defunct Dallas Times Herald, was quickly sent into the streets. He was the first to talk to Abraham Zapruder, the clothing manufacturer who famously filmed the assassination.

You found yourself in the midst of history.

Darwin Payne:

And I knew that. I was very much aware of that.

Jeffrey Brown:

Many years later, he's worried that history, that knowledge is being lost.

Does it sadden you that few people, especially young people, know?

Darwin Payne:

Young people should know the history of their city, of their nation, and of the world.

Jeffrey Brown:

Another young reporter featured of special interest to us, then 29-year-old Jim Lehrer, also with The Times Herald, who was at the airport Love Field when the president and first lady, Jackie Kennedy, arrived, and later at police headquarters where Oswald was being held.

In fact, Jim's friend and "News Hour" co-founder Robert MacNeil was also in Dallas that day covering events for NBC News. Fifty years later, they spoke about it on our program.

Jim Lehrer:

And I was there when they brought in Oswald. And I wrote his name down. I still had the notebook. I was one of those people who asked, hey, did you shoot the president?

Robert MacNeil:

I was also in the police station that evening, and doing reports through NBC, and I saw Oswald paraded back and when he said, "I didn't kill anybody, I'm just a patsy."

Jim Lehrer:

And the guy standing next to me, who I did not know at the time, was Jack Ruby.

Jeffrey Brown:

The intrigue with that day lives on, outside on Dealey Plaza and the famous grassy knoll, another scene, tourists getting quick photos amid traffic on the X markings where JFK was shot, others encountering regulars at the site promoting their books and memorabilia, convinced the official story was a cover-up.

Robert Wilonsky:

This was never my profession. It was always my passion. Started calling witnesses out of the phone book when I was 16, and they talked to me.

Jeffrey Brown:

I was joined by Dallas Morning News columnist Robert Wilonsky, born and raised here, endlessly fascinated by the pull of a place, he says is still Dallas' number one tourist destination.

Robert Wilonsky:

Whether or not we talk about it today, whether or not we think about it today, it defined Dallas. It made us grow up, it made us look inward, and it made us think differently about who we were.

Jeffrey Brown:

At one point, Wilonsky sidled up to a British visitor who said he used to teach American history in London.

Robert Wilonsky:

When you see the guys with the conspiracy theory magazines, what's your take on that?

Man:

Lee Harvey Oswald doing it himself seems a little bit simplistic.

Robert Wilonsky:

Oh.

Man:

Was he involved with someone?

(LAUGHTER)

Robert Wilonsky:

See? You taught American history, but...

Man:

Well, yes, I know.

Jeffrey Brown:

Wilonsky wasn't surprised at all. In fact, he takes it further.

You can in some ways tie today's conspiracy theories of all kinds to this place?

Robert Wilonsky:

Oh, my God, absolutely.

Jeffrey Brown:

Yes.

Robert Wilonsky:

Once you go into one conspiracy, that rabbit hole is large and it is deep and it is wide and it is never-ending. Once you find one conspiracy, you are convinced that everything else that you have been taught and told is incorrect. That begins here for a lot of people, but it certainly doesn't end here.

Jeffrey Brown:

Back inside, museum officials have something quite different on their minds. They recently received an enormous gift.

You have got the negative here of this very famous photograph, right?

Nicola Longford:

This is the original negative of Jack Ruby shooting Lee Harvey Oswald.

Jeffrey Brown:

The Pulitzer Prize-winning image by Dallas Times Herald photojournalist Bob Jackson captured a moment forever tied to the history of the JFK assassination. But Jackson has now given the museum his entire Dallas archive, more than 20,000 original images from the 1960s and '70s, allowing the museum to tell a richer, more comprehensive story of the city itself.

And new funding from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, the federal agency known as the IMLS, will allow the museum to fully research and digitize the collection.

It's part of a hoped-for expansion plan into other floors of the building to broaden the story it's telling, the city then and now.

Nicola Longford:

We want to tell the story of what Dallas was like before the assassination, how it changed afterwards, and how it's continuing to evolve. So, this is really made up the psyche, really, of Dallas, and who we are now and where we're going.

Jeffrey Brown:

In the meantime, there's the continuing image of JFK himself, the loss, says curatorStephen Fagin, inextricably bound up with the promise.

Stephen Fagin:

And he had this uncanny charisma and soaring rhetoric that inspired people around the world. And I do think people find that lacking in the world today.

And so, when they come here, when they write in our memory books, when they share oral histories with us, when they just speak to staff members, we get this sense that they miss what President Kennedy represented, that somehow he represented the best of us, the potential of America.

Jeffrey Brown:

For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Jeffrey Brown in Dallas at the Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza.

Listen to this Segment

Watch the Full Episode

In his more than 30-year career with the News Hour, Brown has served as co-anchor, studio moderator, and field reporter on a wide range of national and international issues, with work taking him around the country and to many parts of the globe. articles.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
articles.description: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
articles.content:
A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit

ByAnbarasan Ethirajan
Global Affairs Correspondent
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

articles.title: Court approves $7.25 billion Bayer settlement over claims Roundup weed killer caused cancer
articles.description: Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.
articles.content:
By —

David A. Lieb, Associated Press David A. Lieb, Associated Press

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/court-approves-7-25-billion-bayer-settlement-over-claims-roundup-weed-killer-caused-cancer

Court approves $7.25 billion Bayer settlement over claims Roundup weed killer caused cancer

Nation Nov 20, 2026 6:25 PM EST

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.

WATCH: What science tells us about the health risks of Roundup

The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness.

For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users.

Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.

Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.

In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation."

The decision could be appealed.

Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years

Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer's deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.

WATCH: U.S. Forest Service, timber companies spraying record amounts of glyphosate in California

The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.

Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it's not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.

About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.

The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.

In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court's precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict "should send a strong signal" that plaintiffs "will face significant challenges" pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer's U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.

Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair

Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February.

"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.

The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000.

Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive.

"This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that's ever been contemplated," attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. He said it locked in future claimants for decades with no chance at punitive damages yet "kept the product that they were exposed to on the market, allowing the victims to continue to be exposed."

The settlement was filed in St. Louis Circuit Court in Missouri, home to Bayer's North America crop science division and the state where many of the lawsuits have been brought.

A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
