articles.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
articles.description: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildoutWho are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it.
articles.content:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

articles.title: MLK's handwritten draft of iconic speech on display for the first time
articles.description: The only known handwritten draft of The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech is on display in his hometown. The iconic phrase, however, never made it on the page.
articles.content:
ATLANTA, GA - THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 2026 - Exterior of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights where King's draft of the speech is displayed. Lynsey Weatherspoon for NPR hide caption

Lynsey Weatherspoon for NPR

ATLANTA – The only known draft of one of the most famous speeches in American history is on public display for the first time: The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s remarks at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963. And it's written in his own hand.

"Just for a few days we have this incredible artifact here, which is Doctor King's handwritten, final draft of what became known as the 'I Have a Dream' speech," said Jill Savitt, CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, King's hometown.

"Nothing has given me chills like this handwritten document, where you see him crafting one of the most iconic speeches in U.S. history."

Sponsor Message

It's written in cursive, blue ink on yellow legal paper. King scratched through entire sections and reworked them, or changed a particular word or phrase.

"You see him on the page wrestling with the words," Savitt said. "He's struggling with: How do you make this case to America that we're not living up to our own ideals?"

The seven-page document, which will be on exhibit here through Sunday, is enclosed in a glass case in a gallery dedicated to the March on Washington. Above the display, footage plays of speeches and the crowd of 250,000 gathered on the National Mall on Aug. 28, 1963.

Savitt said King originally titled the speech "Normalcy Never Again." Notably, the manuscript does not include what became the most famous lines from that day, "I Have a Dream."

"Doctor King improvised that," she said. "The preacher in him connected with a crowd in a particular way. And when you watch footage, you can almost see this electric charge go through him."

His rousing words that day on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial included:

"I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream today."

Sponsor Message

Savitt says King sent the draft to be typed up in the pre-dawn hours from the Willard Hotel in Washington, DC, on the day he was to deliver it.

The handwritten copy of King's speech was discovered by Xernona Clayton, an Atlanta civil rights leader who worked closely with King and his wife, Coretta Scott King. Her late husband, Edward Clayton, was one of King's speechwriters.

Now 96, she said in an interview with NPR Thursday she found the papers tucked in a manilla envelope while cleaning out his old desk.

"I knew Doctor King's handwriting very well, and I said, 'Oh, this can't be the speech,'" she recalled. "Then when I started reading it, I knew that it was and then I got scared. Like, what do I do now?"

That was in the late 1990s, and she tucked it back into the desk. She rediscovered it a couple years ago, and it took her back to 1963.

"As I went through the speech, I was reading his words and hearing them in my head," she said. "Martin Luther King spoke to the world through that speech."

She decided it was time to share the document with the world. Clayton's charitable trust is offering it for auction through Christie's in New York in January, where the auction house says bids could top $10 million. Prior to that, the manuscript also will be on display in Chicago.

Clayton said she wanted it available to the public with the hope that people will find inspiration in King's words today.

"He used to tell me all the time how much he hated that we as a people can't live together," she recalled. "That was his preachment. All of the time he was preoccupied with what can we do to get people to love each other."

Sponsor Message

For former Atlanta Mayor Shirley Franklin, who visited the center last week, seeing the document was personal.

"Do you see me?" she asked, pointing to a photograph on display of the crowd at the March on Washington. "I'm sitting right there by the reflecting pool."

Franklin was Atlanta's mayor from 2002-2010, the first Black woman elected to lead a city in the Deep South.

"It's amazing that 60 years later this document has survived," she said.

Looking at King's writings, Franklin said she was struck by how thoughtful he was about each and every word.

"As brilliant as he was, as clear as he was about what he was trying to accomplish, it required enhancement and refinement," she said. "He was making this speech as good as it could be."

Yet even with all the reviewing and refining, what stuck from that speech never made it on the paper.

"What we remember is the part that came from his heart," Franklin said. "Gives me the chills."

Franklin is a living witness to the change wrought by the work of King and others civil rights pioneers, but she said seeing the speech is a reminder that the work is ongoing.

"Sixty years later, we've made some progress," she said. "Much of what he says is relevant today, because we've not really fulfilled the full promise of a free and a loving community."

Franklin helped found the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta. She said it's fitting such a foundational document got its public debut here.

"This is one of my favorite rooms," she said, as the famous ending of King's speech played on the screen overhead:

"In the words of the old Negro spiritual, 'Free at last, free at last. Thank God almighty we are free at last.'"

Second federal judge blocks construction of Trump's memorial arch

Politics Nov 20, 2026 4:28 PM EST

WASHINGTON (AP) — A second federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump's administration from building a 250-foot memorial arch in the nation's capital, issuing an order on Friday that keeps the construction work on hold indefinitely, according to plaintiffs' lawyers who sued to challenge the project.

READ MORE: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's triumphal arch construction

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, issued her order from the bench in a lawsuit brought by the Arlington County Board. Brinkema ruled two days after a different judge in Washington, D.C., extended a previous order that blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the arch on a more temporary basis.

Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm.

The Virginia board claims Trump's project will exacerbate traffic congestion and jeopardize public safety in the county, which is across the Potomac River from Washington.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," plaintiffs' attorney Kate Talmor said in a statement after Friday's hearing.

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington agreed to extend a temporary restraining order keeping the project on hold until Dec. 3. The injunction issued by Brinkema doesn't have a specified expiration date.

Chutkan initially blocked the arch's construction on Nov. 5, shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy panel giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.

The case before Chutkan was filed on behalf of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit last month, citing the impact the structure would have on Arlington National Cemetery, where family members are buried.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump, a Republican, has pushed in his efforts to leave a personal imprint on Washington's historic landscape. At 250 feet, the arch would be twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial.

Brinkema was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Bill Clinton. Chutkan was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama.

articles.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
articles.description: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
articles.content:
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

ByRachel Clun
Business reporter
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

  • Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

    • Published
      3 days ago

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.content:
Gérard Depardieu and French author investigated over sexual allegations

ByHafsa Khalil
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Warning: this story contains graphic content

French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.

The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.

The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.

Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.

The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.

She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".

French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.

Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".

The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.

The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.

On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.

Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

articles.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
articles.description: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6%Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.Speaking at an event in London on Thur
articles.content:
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.

JP Morgan declined to comment.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
articles.description: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
articles.content:
Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader

ByKayla Epstein, in New York court and Nadine Yousif, Senior Canada reporter
  • Published
    20 November 2026

A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.

The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

  • Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader

    • Published
      14 February

  • Who was Canadian Sikh leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar?

    • Published
      2 October 2023

  • Why are some Sikhs calling for a separate state?

    • Published
      1 December 2023

  • Canada accuses India of role in Sikh leader's murder

    • Published
      19 September 2023

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

Court grants request to prevent military from detonating bomb-making chemicals in Iowa

Nation Nov 20, 2026 2:27 PM EST

DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A federal appeals court has granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa.

The ruling came late Thursday, putting in jeopardy the military's plans to deal with dozens of barrels of lead azide pending further direction by the court.

READ MORE: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals

"The Army can't detonate under the permit while the permit is stayed," said Thien Chau, an attorney with Earthjustice, which filed a petition on behalf of Iowa groups calling for a review of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency permit.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to put out a schedule Friday for when it will issue a ruling on the groups' emergency motion or even if there will be a hearing. Chau said attorneys expect the court will try to decide before Monday's planned operation.

The Army did not immediately return messages seeking comment on how the court action would affect its plans.

The Army has said the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop.

The detonation was initially planned for Friday, but the Army announced Thursday that it would push the operation back to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about the potential health and environmental consequences.

"This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had announced in a post on X.

The Army, the EPA and the federal Department of Health and Human Services followed up Friday with a joint statement saying they were working together to ensure the detonation is conducted in the safest way possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement read.

An inspection earlier this year at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant determined that the lead azide, which is used in munitions production, had started to degrade. The crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.

The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.

The Army detailed its plans during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.

Some schools and businesses had planned to close, as the Army recommended that people stay indoors, bring their pets and livestock inside and keep their windows and doors closed. Officials also urged residents in the path of the predicted plume to clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.

"The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory stated. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals."

Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She said during an interview Thursday that she didn't know if she needed to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond.

"There's just so many details that I feel like haven't been addressed with the public."

Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

articles.title: Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning
articles.description: Christmas comedy hit is set for a follow-up from the point of view of the father with Seth Rogen as writer and producerA Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return.According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni, Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this
articles.content:
A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return.

According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni, Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline, will be from the father’s point of view.

The film will also recruit Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg as writers and producers and they will work with Culkin to craft the script. Rogen and Goldberg recently worked with Disney on a Muppets TV special.

Home Alone was a major box office hit upon release in 1990, grossing $476m worldwide and becoming the year’s second-biggest movie. Culkin returned for the sequel Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which made $359m two years later.

The franchise continued without the actor for three further movies and then in 2021, after Fox had been bought by Disney, there was a straight-to-streaming reboot.

Culkin later reprised the role in a 2018 commercial for Google and this year has once again returned as Kevin for a new McDonald’s advert.

Last year, he was asked about a sequel at an anniversary event.

“I kind of had this idea,” he said. “I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard and I’m not really paying enough attention and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me and then I get locked out.”

In his pitch, the character’s son won’t let him in and would be the one setting the traps with the house as “some sort of metaphor for our relationship”.

The original film’s director, Chris Columbus, who later went on to direct the first two Harry Potter adventures, has spoken out about a possible sequel. “I think it’s a mistake to try to go back and recapture something we did 35 years ago,” he said. “I think it should be left alone.”

Politics Updated on Nov 20, 2026 4:32 PM EST — Published on Nov 20, 2026 2:09 PM EST

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S.

Watch the video in the player above.

Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine, despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict.

"He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But, "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelensky and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it."

During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state.

Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm welcome and repeated references to Putin as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding.

He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf.


Watch the video in the player above.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."

"I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said.

Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace.

"You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies.

"I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats."

Barrow reported from Atlanta.

White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages

ByImran Rahman-Jones
Technology reporter
  • Published

The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".

His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.

US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.

In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.

articles.title: Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
articles.description: Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980sA chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing h
articles.content:
A chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Her trial heard she wore short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

After her conviction she was granted bail and was due to be sentenced at Harrow crown court on Friday.

But Bowen, from Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to court in the morning, and the judge, Karim Ezzat, issued a warrant for her arrest, “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall had earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from Scotchbrook was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, said: “Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn’t answer.”

He had earlier said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

In an update on Friday afternoon, the Met said: “On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing.

“A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.

“At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.

“She has been taken into police custody. A new sentencing date will be set by the court in due course.”

Bowen’s trial heard that she was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

One victim had told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.

The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

articles.title: ‘Worth fighting for’: senators vow to restore financial watchdog agency after Guardian investigation
articles.description: Democrats – including incoming banking chair and both majority leader candidates – said wealthy interests were prioritized over the needs of working AmericansIn response to a Guardian investigation, four US Senate Democrats say they will work to resurrect a financial watchdog agency that has abandon
articles.content:
In response to a Guardian investigation, four US Senate Democrats say they will work to resurrect a financial watchdog agency that has abandoned dozens of enforcement actions under the second Trump administration.

The Guardian found that after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) dropped more than 20 lawsuits against banks and corporations accused of a range of financial misconduct, complaints against those firms rose by an average of more than 75%. In many of these recent complaints, consumers described the same issues the CFPB’s suits had sought to address.

The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren – who first proposed the CFPB’s creation after the 2008 financial crash, and is now poised to become chair of the Senate banking committee in January – promised to investigate the administration’s attempts to weaken the CFPB.

“Donald Trump has sidelined the financial cop on the beat that has returned more than $21bn directly to Americans who were cheated by big banks and giant corporations,” Warren said in a statement.

The Guardian’s reporting, she added, “shows what came next: Trump’s billionaire friends and Wall Street donors getting away with scamming Americans. The next Congress will defend the CFPB, investigate how the Trump administration has abandoned cheated Americans, and put forward legislation to protect consumers and bring down costs.”

Since Trump took office, the CFPB has dramatically scaled back public enforcement actions against companies – even while Americans submit record numbers of complaints to the agency. After filing an average of roughly 30 public enforcement actions each year for more than a decade, the bureau has initiated just one since then director Rohit Chopra, a Joe Biden appointee, was fired on 30 January 2025.

The leadership of the CFPB under the second Trump administration has claimed that the agency has long been harmful to companies and consumers alike. An agency spokesperson asserted in a statement to the Guardian that the CFPB had cost Americans hundreds of billions of dollars – “making the American Dream, like homeownership, more costly by the thousands for each borrower”.

“This Weaponized agency attacked political enemies and disfavored industries and used novel legal theories and secret justifications to ruin lives and businesses,” the statement added. “We are fixing that and bringing the agency back to operating within statute and away from breaking the law and helping all business and Americans who were victims of thuggery.”

The Guardian’s reporting on the agency comes in the wake of midterm elections in which the economy and cost of living concerns were at the top of most voters’ minds.

In response to the investigation, the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, vowed to “make sure that the CFPB is operating at its full capacity” once Democrats gain control of Congress.

“The Trump administration has done everything in its power to bow down to special interests and billionaires at the expense of American families,” Schumer said. “The CFPB was created to make sure that everyday folks could be protected from predatory actors, but Republicans have undermined it at every turn.”

The Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, who announced on 12 November that he would challenge Schumer for the role of Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes, said the CFPB’s rollback demanded greater focus on working Americans.

“The CFPB returned billions of dollars to Americans who were conned and scammed by big corporations,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “Naturally, many billionaires didn’t like that, so they had Trump and his cronies use every tool they could to dismantle an agency whose job is to stand up for working families.”

Van Hollen’s fellow senator from Maryland, Angela Alsobrooks, also weighed in.

“The CFPB works for the American people,” she said. “The CFPB is worth fighting for.”
articles.author: Sophie Sullivan

articles.title: Lauren Boebert says Trump ‘did some things to hurt’ her constituents
articles.description: Controversial Colorado Republican narrowly lost House seat in midterms but says ‘I’m not mad at the president’Lauren Boebert says Donald Trump “did some things that hurt” her constituents before they voted the pugnacious Colorado Republican out of her US House seat during midterm elections, which sa
articles.content:
Lauren Boebert says Donald Trump “did some things that hurt” her constituents before they voted the pugnacious Colorado Republican out of her US House seat during midterm elections, which saw her and the president’s party lose control of Congress.

“This could be a referendum on President Trump,” Boebert said to the Associated Press in an interview published on Friday. “It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican party. I think it’s all of it.

“I’m not mad at the president. [But] the president did some things that hurt my voters.”

Boebert expressed those thoughts during some of her first comments to the news media after Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher defeated her by less than a 1% margin in a race called 10 days after the polls closed.

The conservative firebrand who first joined Congress in 2021 had widely been favored to win a fourth consecutive term. But low approval ratings for Trump after he started the war in Iran, pursuing an aggressive mass deportation campaign and other unpopular initiatives created an environment in which Democrats flipped nine seats in the US Senate and about four dozen in the House – including Boebert’s.

In Friday’s interview, Boebert pinned some of the blame for that outcome on the agenda that Trump set for the first half of his second presidency. But she also said, “it’s all of the Republican party,” which had majorities in both congressional chambers dating back to the latter part of Joe Biden’s lone Oval Office term.

“I think it’s more all of us,” Boebert told the AP, alluding to high fuel prices after the Iran war, Republican infighting and unfulfilled promises. “We had solutions, and we didn’t take action.”

Boebert navigated various controversies throughout her time in Congress, which began with her supporting Trump’s lies that the 2020 election that he lost to Biden was unduly rigged by fraudsters.

A 2023 scandal saw her and a man with whom she was on a date get kicked out of a performance of the stage production Beetlejuice in Denver for inappropriate behavior, including vaping and groping each other. She later apologized for the conduct, which was recorded on surveillance video, saying: “I simply fell short of my values.”

Just weeks before her contest against Laubacher, an ethics complaint filed against her accused her of having sexual relationships with three staffers, including one who was paid to stay silent. She denied the allegations cited in the complaint, which she dismissed as “politically motivated”.

Boebert’s interview with the AP on Friday was not the first time she has spoken out against Trump. Notably, she was among the Congress members who most loudly called for the full disclosure of files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite – even after the Trump administration tried to convince her to drop her support for a measure that would compel such a release.

Trump responded to Boebert by calling her “dumb”. He also kicked off his second presidency by vetoing a Boebert-sponsored bill that would have funded a drinking water project in her district after the legislation unanimously cleared the House and Senate.

That prompted a critical statement from Boebert saying: “If this administration wants to make its legacy blocking projects that deliver water to rural Americans, that’s on them.”

Boebert struck a more conciliatory tone in Friday’s interview with the AP, remarking, “I respect President Trump, I still work with him, I want to continue to work with him. Not for him, with him.”

She only referred to her future plans in vague terms, telling the outlet: “Too many people come to Congress and get rich. I am not one of those. I’m gonna go make some money now.”
articles.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas

articles.description: Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service.

Northeastern Florida now under flood threats from heavy rain that has devastated coastal communities

Nation Nov 20, 2026 1:46 PM EST

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns

"Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected," the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. "In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger."

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.

"Never seen such a thing like this in Florida," said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week's storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.

Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.

Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

articles.title: Florida mechanic found guilty of murdering British woman who attorney says came to US to die
articles.description: Dwain Hall was convicted of stabbing Sonia Exelby, a music teacher who prosecutors say suffered from mental illnessA Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States.Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver,
articles.content:
A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States.

Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver, groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US.

Hall had pleaded not guilty to the charges of kidnap and first-degree murder.

At trial, jurors heard from several witnesses, most of them law enforcement officials, who detailed Hall’s email, phone records, social media accounts and other records to trace his movements after Exelby travelled from the UK to meet him.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. Investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.

The authorities said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from the Gainesville airport in central Florida.

He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

According to the Times, Junior Barrett, Hall’s attorney, argued that Exelby took her own life. “She came here with the intention of dying, she thought she was worthless, useless, a burden on other people,” he said in his closing statement.

“This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle. The fact he did not stop her from killing herself does not make it murder.”

Prosecutor Amy Beth Berndt said jurors should use their “common sense”. She added that Hall targeted Exelby for her mental illness and killed her for his sadistic pleasure.

Berndt said Exelby “was beautiful. She was kind and she was deeply loved by everyone who knew her. And she also suffered from mental illness for most of her life. She should be alive today.”

She added: “No one could save her from the defendant, the ‘Alpha Sadist’. He took advantage of a severely depressed, mentally ill woman who was incapable of making any rational decisions.”

After the verdict was read, Exelby’s brother Barry Wilton said: “This last year has been one of the hardest of our lives. Losing our dear sister Sonia has had a profound impact on me and my entire family. I’m not sure we will ever be the same again.”

Wilton then addressed Hall directly, adding: “You pretended to care for Sonia. You didn’t at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies. You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us.”

In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978

articles.title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
articles.description: Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition requestIn a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house own
articles.content:
In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.

The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.

“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.
articles.author: Timothy Pratt

articles.title: Princeton doctoral student reportedly detained by ICE on way back from conference
articles.description: Eva Yi Xie was taken into custody at Washington DC airport after presenting research at neuroscience conferenceA Princeton University doctoral student has reportedly been taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traveling to Washington DC, for a neuroscience conferenc
articles.content:
A Princeton University doctoral student has reportedly been taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traveling to Washington DC, for a neuroscience conference.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year PhD candidate at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained Thursday at a Washington-area airport, according to university officials and her colleagues.

The Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, reported that Xie is believed to be held at an immigration detention facility in Chantilly, Virginia.

The Brody Lab, a Princeton neuroscience research group, identified Ronald Reagan National airport as the location of her detention in a post on X. According to the lab, Xie had been returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she presented a research poster, when immigration authorities detained her.

Princeton has since secured legal representation for Xie, university spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss confirmed to the Daily Princetonian.

The detention also prompted a late-night message to graduate students from Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. Priestley sent the email to students at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute late Thursday night, acknowledging the situation and outlining the university’s response.

“We hope she is able to soon resume her studies at Princeton,” the email, obtained by the Daily Princetonian, read. “Please be assured that we will stay in close contact with the student’s family, her legal team, and her PNI colleagues as this situation is resolved.”

Xie’s current immigration status has not been publicly disclosed.

Xie moved to the US from China in 2016. She earned degrees in computer science and mathematics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, alongside a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio.

Her professional experience includes internships at Meta, Microsoft AI and IBM Research, among other organizations. At Princeton, her doctoral work focuses on the “neural basis of decision-making,” according to the Daily Princetonian.

The Guardian has reached out to ICE and Princeton for comment.

Xie’s detention comes amid an aggressive nationwide immigration enforcement campaign under Donald Trump, whose administration has made mass deportations a defining priority.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) figures show that ICE deported 483,200 people and conducted more than 491,000 immigration arrests during fiscal year 2026, setting new annual records for the agency.

The Trump administration maintains that its enforcement efforts are intended to uphold immigration laws and remove dangerous offenders from the country. However, federal figures and independent reviews indicate that substantial numbers of people kept in ICE detention have no criminal convictions.

The enforcement campaign has affected international students and immigrants who originally entered the US legally. Xie’s detention now joins a string of prominent immigration cases that have drawn worldwide scrutiny and raised serious questions about the administration’s tactics.

Among those cases is Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University student detained by immigration agents in Massachusetts last year. Videos of Öztürk’s arrest spread rapidly online, drawing widespread attention to the administration’s treatment of international students.

She was among numerous foreign students targeted over pro-Palestinian expression and protest during demonstrations against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Those protests have been particularly prominent on American university campuses.

Another high-profile case involved Mahmoud Khalil, a 30-year-old Palestinian permanent resident and Columbia University graduate student who emerged as a leading figure in campus protests last year.

Khalil was arrested without due process in front of his pregnant wife and subsequently detained at an immigration facility. Authorities denied him permission to leave detention to attend the birth of his child.

The administration’s enforcement policies also came under intense scrutiny after the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been living in Maryland. Ábrego García was deported from the US to El Salvador in March 2025, despite the Trump administration’s admission that the removal was an error.
articles.author: Marina Dunbar in New York

articles.title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
articles.description: A federal judge in Virginia said she will issue a preliminary injunction against Trump's arch, going a step further than the D.C. federal judge who temporarily blocked construction earlier this week.
articles.content:
President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week. John McDonnell/AP hide caption

John McDonnell/AP

A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

Politics

Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.

Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.

The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Sponsor Message

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."

Politics

Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave

The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.

"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.

Sponsor Message

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.

On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.

Politics

Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?

That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.

Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.

And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.

She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.

National

D.C. airspace is complicated. Experts say Trump's arch would add one more risk

"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.

Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.

The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.
articles.author: Rachel Treisman
