articles.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
articles.description: PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hopeSeveral sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the
articles.content:
Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”

For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.

More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.

While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.

Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.
articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent

articles.title: Two men killed after glider crashes into Loch Leven in Scotland
articles.description: The pair had taken off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at nearby Portmoak on a training flightTwo men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emer
articles.content:
Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.

Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday.

The force said next of kin had been told and the incident was not being treated as suspicious. Two HM Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance were sent to the scene, along with a fire service appliance and a specialist crew.

The pair had taken off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak airfield near the loch’s eastern shore in a Perkoz two-person glider on a training flight.

A spokesperson for the gliding centre said: “The incident is currently under investigation by the Air Accident Investigation Branch [AAIB] of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

“Our club is cooperating fully with these organisations. At the present time, there is no indication as to the cause of the accident.”

An AAIB spokesperson said: “A multidisciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to gather evidence and make inquiries.”

The police said airspace restrictions had been put in place after the crash was reported.

articles.title: No one else in Reform is suitable to lead the party, Nigel Farage says
articles.description: Farage issues warning to potential rivals and says he will fight next election as leader if ‘still here and fit and healthy’Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.The Reform
articles.content:
Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.

The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe.

There has been speculation over Farage’s future in light of police and parliamentary investigations of Reform’s financial affairs. The Commons standards watchdog is due to report soon on whether he should have declared a £5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. If he gets a substantial suspension from parliament, he could face a second byelection, contested by other main parties, in his Clacton constituency.

However, Farage sounded a note of defiance in an interview with the Sun, saying: “These are very thoughtful moments, but, you know what, if I’m not here doing this job right now, who else could? Who else would? I don’t see that person. So I’m gonna do it.”

A number of other Reform UK politicians are potential contenders to succeed him, including the party’s economics spokesperson and former Conservative, Robert Jenrick, the home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, and the former leader Richard Tice. Another possibility is the return of Rupert Lowe, who left Reform in acrimonious circumstances and founded his own party, Restore Britain, but who is popular on the online hard right.

The party is going through a difficult period after slipping from first place in the polls to second or third behind behind Labour and sometimes the Conservatives.

Asked by the Sun if he had “blown” his chances of reaching No 10, Farage said: “No, far from it.”

He admitted there had been “self-inflicted wounds” in the past year but said he still had a chance of becoming prime minister.

He told the newspaper that he would fight the next election as Reform leader if he was “still here and fit and healthy”.

He also batted away questions about the £5m, which he has insisted was to pay for his personal security despite the fact the party has been providing this.

“What’s it got to do with you? Drugs, sports cars, desert islands. It’s a gift,” he said, adding that although the party had had “ebbs and flows” and had made mistakes after growing “too far and too fast”, he was confident it was “more than through the worst of it”.

On the prospect of another battle over Europe as Andy Burnham weighs the case for rejoining the EU, the Reform leader said: “If you ask me, have I got the energy and the enthusiasm to do this again? I would say to you, hold my jacket. I’m ready for it.”

He also warned of people taking to the streets with “direct action” if Brexit is reversed.

In a separate interview with the Times while travelling to Brussels, where Burnham was attempting a reset deal, Farage said he believed the issue of Europe would dominate the years to come.

“It’s going to be absolutely huge. It’s going to be much bigger than anyone realises. The genie is out of the bottle; it literally can’t be stopped now,” he said.

He also ruled out joining a new campaign called Stay Out, led by former Tories, suggesting he would make his own case for keeping Brexit.
articles.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor

articles.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
articles.description: President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UKSenior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six m
articles.content:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.”

articles.title: Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded
articles.description: Just like bad weather, air travel disruptions irritate many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.
articles.content:
By —

Deepti Hajela, Associated Press Deepti Hajela, Associated Press

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/travelers-concerns-spike-as-thanksgiving-nears-and-tech-hiccups-grow-but-few-are-dissuaded

Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded

Nation Nov 20, 2026 12:58 PM EST

NEW YORK (AP) — At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a rare nationwide ground stop last week — the longest since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

READ MORE: White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

"For a lot of people, especially as they're paying attention and because it's in the news where they're tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we're having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious," said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.

It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.

But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

"For the most part, air travel still remains strong," said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People "might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it."

Air travel is vital — and taken for granted

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

"Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted," said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

"You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places," he said. "But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It's a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that's a clear sign of its success — that you're in a bus."

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it.

READ MORE: Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal?

"I literally haven't had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I'm like, just, okay, here's another thing," said Jolene, who lives in Miami.

She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, "the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday."

And instead of flying this year, they'll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. "But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there's just not much choice. What are you going to do?"

The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays

If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.

Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.

It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines' online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.

The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it's a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn't go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage

"The funny part," she said, "is we have to buy toilet paper anyway."

AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

articles.title: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
articles.description: Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as
articles.content:
Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

But the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Burnham rejected suggestions there was any confusion over the deals coming into force: “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” he said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.

Hailing the “historic” agreement Burnham said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe,” as he argued that the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

The prime minister said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, while also reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal. The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those might be. It will be to inform the next parliament.”

Burnham also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who was in Brussels on Friday to hold a retaliatory press conference, to justify why they would reject a deal which, he said, would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity. “Why would anybody turn their back on that?”

The prime minister said the deals, which were initiated by Keir Starmer, would add 0.5% to British GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Farage said Burnham had been naive and the EU had “used this moment to strongarm the British prime minister over tuition fee cuts for hundreds of thousands of EU students”.

EU leaders sought to play down differences over tuition fees. “We are heading in the same direction and that is what matters,” the European Council president, António Costa, said of the broad relationship. He described the UK as “our closest neighbour, a reliable ally and a natural partner”.

Von der Leyen said it was up to the UK to decide where the journey was going, adding: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

In a sign of tension in the negotiations, the EU agreed a declaration that the three deals would not come into force without equal treatment on fees for EU students at British universities.

“The [EU] Council and [European] Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students,” stated the confidential statement seen by the Guardian. The EU would not adopt the three agreements before “the conclusions of the negotiations … providing for equal treatment on tuition fees”, it added.

Another potential flashpoint could be the UK’s status as a rule-taker. The food and drink and emissions trading deals require the UK to align with EU rules. British experts will be invited to relevant EU meetings, including dealing with potential animal health emergencies. But Britain will not have voting rights. Burnham rejected suggestions this was a fig leaf, saying it would be “quite a moment” to have British experts back in EU meeting rooms.

France was said to be instrumental in shaping Britain’s exclusion, although Paris argues its position was widely supported and reflects the reality that a non-member state cannot be a decision-maker.

Following the talks, Burnham was invited to a lunch of pea and mint soup, battered North Sea cod and chips, followed by Brussels waffle with fruit.

The summit began with a highly choreographed welcome ceremony in the Europa “space egg” European Council building, where a quintet played the British and EU anthems.

The UK hailed a joint decision to create a “partnership for economic resilience”, as an answer to its concerns over the EU’s Made in Europe plans. The EU is still finalising legislation that will give EU companies preference when public money is spent on the key technologies, such as renewables and electric cars. The UK has been arguing for Britain to be included in Made in Europe to ensure UK firms are not locked out of European supply chains.

In response, the two sides agreed to set up “a common prosperity and economic security space”, essentially an answer to shared concerns about artificially cheap Chinese goods that are depressing prices across Europe. But questions over whether the UK needs to align with EU trade defences remain open. Burnham said the two sides had reached an agreement “to work together where we have common threats”.

In an echo of the Brexit years, the final deal emerged after late-night talks went to the wire.

The German Social Democrat MEP Bernd Lange called on both sides to resolve the tuition fees issue to make studying affordable in a way that works for universities: “We can’t open the door to young people and then price them out of walking through it.”

The EU has welcomed Burnham’s breaking of taboos over rejoining, but also voiced frustration at British negotiating tactics. “The UK has a tendency to make even small questions so difficult,” an EU diplomat said. “A British prime minister talks about a change of approach … Then in negotiations it seems like British negotiators act the same way they always had.”
articles.author: Jennifer Rankin and Peter Walker in Brussels

articles.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
articles.description: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
articles.content:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham

ByRichard Wheeler
Political reporter
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

  • Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

    • Published
      3 days ago

  • What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

    • Published
      3 days ago

  • Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

    • Published
      3 days ago

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

'Brainstorming process'

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

'Endless betrayal'

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.content:
By —

Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/mamdani-sets-plan-to-close-nycs-notorious-rikers-island-jail-by-2032

Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail by 2032

Nation Nov 20, 2026 12:31 PM EST

NEW YORK (AP) — New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.

READ MORE: Mamdani hits 100 days as mayor of New York City

The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.

For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing " abnormal and unacceptable " conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.

Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.

At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers "a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on."

"The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through," he said.

The plan centers on a goal of lowering the city's inmate population from the around 6,700 people currently housed at Rikers to a little over 4,000.

The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays so people spend less time behind bars.

"Our nation has a very real mass incarceration problem," the mayor said. "We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head on."

Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers — an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport — the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment. The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programs.

The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall. The new deadlines require approval from the New York City Council.

Julie Menin, speaker of the City Council, praised the mayor's plan at the news conference, saying that after years of delay "we are finally getting back on track."

The City Council voted to close the jail complex in 2019 and replace it with newer jails located in the city's boroughs by 2027. At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

Sales of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' hit more than $2.3 billion after long-anticipated release

Arts Nov 20, 2026 12:06 PM EST

Sales of "Grand Theft Auto VI" are skyrocketing, as gamers' insatiable appetite for the series continues.

WATCH: Why Grand Theft Auto VI's release is a major cultural moment

The game, which launched on Thursday, has hit $2.36 billion in revenue with approximately 24.6 million units sold, according to Sensor Tower, which is a market research firm that tracks mobile apps, digital advertising and consumer behavior online.

Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that "GTA VI" was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day.

"GTA VI" is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.

It's the first new "GTA" game in 13 years, with the story of "GTA VI" centered on a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime. Early reviews for the game have noted that it has a depth of relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups and bank robberies.

The "Grand Theft Auto" franchise has sold more than 470 million units globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

articles.title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
articles.description: Less than half of Republicans nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling.
articles.content:
A firefighter walks past voting booths at a firehouse serving as a polling location in Detroit on Nov. 3. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption

Spencer Platt/Getty Images

President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.

Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.

Loading...

In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.

While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.

"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."

Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.

But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.

"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."

Sponsor Message

Voting

GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election

Voting

The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue

The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.

On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.

Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.

"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"

But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.

The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."

"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."

Sponsor Message

To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.

"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.

But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.

The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.description: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
articles.content:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk

ByPhoebe Hopson and Paul Kirby, Europe digital editor
  • Published
    20 November 2026, 12:09 GMT
Updated 2 hours ago

Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Latest botched execution prompts calls for US moratorium on lethal injections
articles.description: Reinaldo Dennes screamed in pain and took over an hour to die – but Texas officials branded the execution a successA botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a
articles.content:
A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a nationwide moratorium that would pause all lethal injections.

It took 63 minutes for Reinaldo Dennes, 70, to be proclaimed dead in the Huntsville penitentiary. The execution team had struggled to find a vein through which a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital could be administered.

Descriptions of the botched lethal injection bear chilling similarities to the recent failed execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike who in September became the only person ever to survive a full dose of execution drugs. Both Dennes and Pike were subjected to lethal injection protocols using pentobarbital, in both cases staff struggled to establish intravenous lines, and in both the prisoner expressed experiencing excruciating pain and burning sensations.

“The world saw what happened to Christa Pike, and now to Mr Dennes,” said Robin Maher, executive director of the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center. “The question now is, how many more of these botched executions will be tolerated by the American people?”

A harrowing eyewitness account of the night’s events was given by the prisoner’s spiritual adviser, the Rev Jeff Hood, who stood beside the gurney with his hand on Dennes’s shoulder. Hood describes how for up to five minutes Dennes fought against the pain.

“The pain!” Dennes shouted, according to Hood’s account.

“My leg, my leg, my leg,” he screamed, adding that his leg was “on fire”.

Hood writes in his account that Dennes “shifted on the gurney, back and forth, back and forth. He contorted. He grabbed hold of the leather straps and pulled against them until his body lifted. His shoulder drove up into my palm. Then it fell away. Then it drove up again. Twice he screamed, ‘It’s not working like it’s supposed to. Fuck. Fuck. Fuck. What is going on? Fuck. Fuck. Fuck.’”

Throughout the ordeal, Hood reports, the prisoner continued to pray, begging for an end to it.

“Take me home, Father. I don’t think this is normal. Take me, Father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”

Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was shot and killed in Houston.

Maya Foa, chief executive of the human rights group Reprieve, called for a moratorium on lethal injections. She said: “Lethal injection is torture – and Reinaldo Dennes was not sentenced to be tortured. Even the most ardent supporters of capital punishment must recognise that the dominant method of execution in the US is broken and cannot be allowed to continue.”

The Texas department of criminal justice insisted that the execution went fully according to plan. Its spokeswoman, Amanda Hernandez, told the New York Times that “as far as this agency is concerned, it is 100 percent not a botched execution. This was a successful execution, and we did follow all of the proper protocols to do it correctly.”

But such a blanket dismissal of any concerns failed to dampen a chorus of criticism. “Americans are now seeing the harsh reality of the death penalty, and I just don’t know how much longer state officials think they can double down on a story that is false,” Maher said.

Texas has been under the spotlight for many years for the way it obtains and stores its stocks of lethal execution drugs, a manoeuvre which it is careful to shroud in secrecy in an attempt to avoid public scrutiny. In the wake of an international boycott, the state’s prison service has taken to buying pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies that make up the chemicals to order.

Lawyers for condemned prisoners have long argued that the supplies can be of variable quality and are often held by the state beyond their expiration dates, running the risk of causing excruciating deaths.

The way that Texas conducts executions is likely to come under fresh review given the political upheaval that the state has experienced in the midterm elections. Not only did the governor’s mansion fall to the Democrat Gina Hinojosa, but Democrats flipped 20 state House seats as well as taking all seats up for election in the Texas supreme court and court of criminal appeals that have enormous power over capital cases.

Jonathan Groner, an expert on execution methods and emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University, said that the Dennes execution illustrated why lethal injections were a “medical charade”. He said: “They imitate general anesthesia which is done in hospitals across the country thousands of times a day, by people with expertise, but when it is done in the death chamber without necessary equipment or skills, people suffer.”

Groner said that the location of the two IV lines placed in Dennes’s body – in a foot and in his shoulder – indicated that the execution team was struggling. “Placing IVs in the neck is very painful and difficult, and a last resort; and the foot is not a top choice because there is a long way to the heart for the medication to be circulated.”

He added: “It’s time for the medical profession to make a stand on executions. People are being tortured. We need to stop, and take a hard look at why we are still doing this.”

articles.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
articles.description: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
articles.content:
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

By
Faisal Islam
Economics editor
  • Published
    20 November 2026

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

articles.title: How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
articles.description: Orchestra Noir is back on tour, selling out stages across the country and proving classical music can be anything you want it to be.
articles.content:
Orchestra Noir was founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers. The all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Andre Calder hide caption

Andre Calder

Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.

The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.

Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.

Sponsor Message
YouTube

In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.

"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."

But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.

Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.

"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.

The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.

Shondalla Calder plays the violin during an Orchestra Noir performance for their The Culture 2000s tour. Andre Calder hide caption

Andre Calder

"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."

Sponsor Message

"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.

When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."

"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."

The journey to the stage

Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.

Nicole Wright on violin while Tiffany Goode plays the trumpet at the ensemble's D.C. performance. Andre Calder hide caption

Andre Calder

Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.

Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.

"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.

Sponsor Message

On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.

"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.

A night to remember

By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.

Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.

Orchestra Noir founder, Jason Ikeem Rodgers conducts the band while they wear their custom black-and-red letter jackets. Andre Calder hide caption

Andre Calder

They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.

When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.

Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.

As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.

"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."

Sponsor Message

"We're being seen. We have something to say," he added. "Younger folk, older folk — they can say, okay, we see Black people playing in orchestras. Which is a serious thing."

Rhandal Jackson and Tiffany Goode play the trumpet. Andre Calder hide caption

Andre Calder

For Wright, who grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, the ensemble has built a musical bridge she always wished existed.

"When I stepped outside, I was hearing Beyoncé or Brandy," she said. "But when I was practicing in the house, I was practicing Vivaldi." "We come to the edge of the stage, we can meet as many audience members as we can and we talk to them," Wright said. "Some of their children are playing the violin or the viola, and they'll ask us to take a picture or they'll ask us to make a video to inspire their daughter. Because sometimes when their daughter is practicing, they don't get to see the end result. Because practicing can take quite a bit of time. So they want us to show their daughters and send these videos to them to help inspire them."

"My goal is making sure [audience members] leave feeling something awesome or something great," Wright added. "And that's what we're doing. We treat every show as if it's our last."

articles.title: Great horned owl survives 70 miles stuck in a moving truck
articles.description: ‘It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen.’The post Great horned owl survives 70 miles stuck in a moving truck appeared first on Popular Science.
articles.content:
In March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill. During a strangely similar scenario, the same wildlife center in Pennsylvania recently treated a great horned owl (Bubo virginianus) who also got jammed in the front of a vehicle. But this one was dragged along for 70 miles. 

“This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.  

The wildlife center’s team received a voicemail from cargo and freight company Old Dominion Freight Line, saying that one of their drivers in Pennsylvania had hit an owl. When they called back, they discovered that the owl was alive and had gotten stuck in the truck’s air dam. The company’s maintenance team was able to remove the owl, but something was clearly wrong with the bird because it couldn’t fly away.

The wildlife team told them to place the injured animal in a dark and quiet place. Ultimately, transport volunteers were able to transfer the owl to Raven Ridge, where the team had waited to receive the patient past the wildlife center’s closing hours. Its feathers were a mess, but the staff was shocked to find no broken wings or legs, nor open wounds. The owl had just injured its left eye. 

But when they called back the next day, “the story got even more incredible,” according to the wildlife center. The driver had felt the collision, but she didn’t know that the owl had gotten stuck on the truck, so she’d continued driving all the way back to the terminal. 

“The distance from the spot where the owl was hit to the terminal was 70 miles,” the team wrote.“The owl was stuck headfirst in the fiberglass air dam for 70 miles at 65 miles per hour. It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen.”

Staff brought the hardy survivor to their vet for an eye exam, which revealed blood and swelling in the injured eye. The wildlife team is now monitoring the bird’s recovery. 

“The owl is doing great, and the left eye that sustained the damage is also healing. After we move the owl outside into a flight cage, we will make sure that the owl can sustain flight, that there are no obvious underlying issues, and that it can find the food placed in its cage,” Young concludes. 

The goal is to ultimately release it close to where the collision occurred.

articles.title: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases
articles.description: The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya.
articles.content:
By —

Mike Corder, Associated Press Mike Corder, Associated Press

Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases

World Nov 20, 2026 11:03 AM EST

THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — The United Nations' top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority.

The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya.

WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya

The World Court has more cases on its docket dealing with alleged breaches of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including a politically charged case about Israel's actions in Gaza.

1. Bosnia-Serbia: The Srebrenica genocide

What happened: The Srebrenica massacre was a peak in the violence of Bosnia's 1992-95 war, which came after the breakup of Yugoslavia unleashed nationalist passions and territorial ambitions across the region.

On July 11, 1995, Serbs overran Srebrenica, at the time a U.N.-protected safe area. They separated at least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from their wives, mothers and sisters and slaughtered them. Those who tried to escape were chased through the woods and over the mountains around town.

How the court ruled: The court, basing itself in part on verdicts at a United Nations war crimes tribunal, said in a 2007 ruling that the Srebrenica killings amounted to genocide. However, it did not find Serbia responsible. It did find Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide. That obligation is enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention.

2. Croatia-Serbia: Attacks on Croatian regions

What happened: In another war that erupted out of the messy breakup of Yugoslavia, Serb forces attacked several regions of neighboring Croatia, killing and wounding Croat citizens. Croatia accused Serbia of controlling forces responsible for attacks from 1991-95 that Zagreb said amounted to genocide.

How the court ruled: In a 2015 decision, the court said that it found genocidal acts, but it said it did not establish genocidal intent. Under the Genocide Convention, intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part, is necessary for a finding of genocide.

3. South Africa-Israel: The Gaza conflict

What happened: Israel launched a devastating military campaign in Gaza following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when militants stormed through Israeli communities, killing some 1,200 people and taking around 250 people hostage.

WATCH: UN's highest court hears request from South Africa on Israel's offensive in Rafah

The Israeli campaign has laid waste to much of the Gaza Strip and killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive, a claim Israel vehemently denies. At public hearings, Israel insisted that its war in Gaza was a legitimate defense of its people and that it was Hamas militants who were guilty of genocide.

How the court ruled: In a 2024 interim ruling, the court ordered Israel to do all it can to prevent death, destruction and any acts of genocide in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the fact that the court was willing to discuss the genocide charges was a "mark of shame that will not be erased for generations."

There has been no ruling yet on the merits of the case and won't be for years. Israel has until May 2029 to file written arguments and only then can the court schedule public hearings. A final ruling could only come months or years after hearings.

Professor Janina Dill, an Oxford University expert on international law and the use of force, said in a statement that the Myanmar ruling "is very instructive of how the Court approaches some of the crucial questions that it faces in other pending genocide cases, including the polarising case of South Africa versus Israel."

She said the 9-6 majority in the Myanmar genocide and a number of separate and dissenting opinions from judges "highlight the lingering doctrinal complexities."

4. Ukraine-Russia: Moscow's war on Ukraine

What happened: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, after earlier illegally annexing the Crimea peninsula.

Shortly after the invasion, Ukraine filed a case accusing Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack. Kyiv argues that those claims amount to a breach of the Genocide Convention.

How the court ruled: The court has already thrown out much of the case. Judges said they have jurisdiction to rule on a request by Ukraine for a declaration that Kyiv is not responsible for genocide, but not on other aspects of the case. Like the South Africa-Israel case, this is at an early stage of proceedings and no final decision on the merits is expected for years.

articles.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
articles.description: Police officials called for "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
articles.content:
Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months

ByKhanyisile Ngcobo
Reporting fromJohannesburg
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.

This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.

The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.

In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.

The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.

The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.

Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.

It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.

  • Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

    • Published
      19 September

Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.

According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.

The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.

The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.

On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.

General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.

The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.

Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.

The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.

He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.

Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.

Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.

In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.

Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".
