articles.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
articles.description: Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year in Anton Chekhov's play, The Seagull, in the US.
articles.content:
Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label

ByAngharad Thomas
BBC Wales
  • Published
    20 November 2026

Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.

Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.

Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.

She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.

The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.

Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".

"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.

Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.

Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.

"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.

"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.

"The Gower Peninsula is breathtaking."

She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".

"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

articles.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
articles.description: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
articles.content:
Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force

ByTom Espiner and Anuk Weerawardana, Business reporters
  • Published
    20 November 2026

New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away.

Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing."

But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?"

  • Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules

    • Published
      21 October

  • No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

    • Published
      1 November

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.

The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.

Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.

Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

articles.title: Iran war has permanently reshaped energy priorities, IEA report says
articles.description: The repercussions from the Iran war will "leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis.
articles.content:
By —

Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

By —

Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press

  • https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-war-has-permanently-reshaped-energy-priorities-iea-report-says

Iran war has permanently reshaped energy priorities, IEA report says

World Nov 20, 2026 10:28 AM EST

The greatest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns are reshaping how the world will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, said an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.

Grow your mind

Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology.

Form error message goes here.

Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm.

The repercussions from the Iran war will "leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis.

Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said, which will benefit renewable technologies, like solar energy, and other alternatives, like nuclear power. But it also reinforces the case to keep coal as a backup for times of crisis.

This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where about a fifth of the world's traded oil flowed.

The report looks "past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today's upheaval," said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, who warned that "the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be."

"I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before," he said.

READ MORE: Iran widens Gulf attacks by targeting U.S. air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain

The annual United Nations climate talks in Turkey, known as COP31, are in their final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are major issues at COP31.

"For the first time, we are actually seeing the policies used to respond to energy security concerns being very strongly aligned with policies needed for energy transitions," said IEA Director of Sustainability Laura Cozzi in an interview with The Associated Press. "This is a unique convergence that sees electrification at the heart of crisis response."

Flagship report projects energy future

The IEA is the world's leading intergovernmental energy organization, with more than 30 member countries. Its flagship report this year analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries stick with current policies or drastically shift because of ongoing crises.

There is a clear before and after the Iran war for the energy sector, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets.

"When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change," said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember.

Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures, and the IEA said the "drive to diversify" fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade.

"The world will not look the same after this crisis, but how we will look exactly, this still depends, and we will see in the next few months," Cozzi said.

The IEA projects the Middle East will still be the world's largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA projects the amount of oil passing the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035.

While fossil fuels still dominate energy mixes, the IEA said solar and nuclear power are the "biggest beneficiaries" of governments prioritizing domestic energy sources.

"This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence," said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. "It's crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home."

READ MORE: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe

Energy security concerns, however, may lead nations to rely on coal as a fallback option. Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association, said "for coal-rich economies, domestic coal remains an important energy security asset."

"We see coal has a momentum," said the IEA's Birol. "We will see if it is long-lived or not."

Climate talks eye electrification

COP31 follows a year rattled by the Iran war, as well as several climate-induced disasters, like Europe's deadly heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding. Global warming is adding pressure to rising electricity demand.

In what the IEA called a "striking milestone," energy demand for cooling overtook energy demand for heating for the first time this year. Cozzi said this is "the beginning of the trend that will last for the next decade and beyond."

India, the world's most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than anywhere else in the world. China, already one of the world's most electrified economies, may see electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035, the highest among major economies.

At COP31, Turkey wants the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

While Turkey prefers this to come from renewables, U.N. documents on the negotiating table don't spell this out. That means power plants running on coal and other fossil fuels could be used to supply power grids, at least initially.

"The IEA's latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy," said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31.

articles.title: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results
articles.description: At a White House press conference Friday, Trump offered little in actual results of the meetings, beyond a joint statement on unity over some issues.
articles.content:
President Trump speaks as Secretary of State Marco Rubio listens during a news briefing at the White House on Friday. Trump is addressing the media after returning from a visit to China where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

President Trump took to the White House briefing room Friday telling reporters his trip to Asia this week – where he met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin – was a resounding success, despite offering few tangible results.

"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," Trump said, standing at the podium with VIce President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio behind him.

But the trip resulted more in agreements to continue discussions rather than any concrete changes. The meeting with Putin and Xi, though historic as it was the first time they met, only resulted in an agreement to continue discussing reducing nuclear risks.

Sponsor Message

In Manila, where Trump met with allies before he traveled to China, Trump signed a trade agreement with Thailand. But there are still details to the deal being finalized and the document signed simply marked a "substantial conclusion" in negotiations.

Diplomacy

Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance

At the White House, Trump gave a wide-ranging opening statement to the press that veered from recounting his trip and who he met with, to asides about Iran, the U.S. Federal Reserve, his quest for a Nobel Peace Prize and domestic manufacturing. It was the first time he took questions from the press since being in China.

One significant change Trump announced in the middle of his press remarks was that he and XI have agreed to establish "joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence – a new move from Trump, who has been adamant that regulation over the technology would inhibit US innovation and help China lead in the global AI race. No further details about what the guardrails would look like, when they would be negotiated and released and how they would be applied between the two nations has been announced.

Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."

Sponsor Message

The announcement of future guardrails comes as Trump is facing headwinds from growing tech outages in the U.S. that ultimately led to Trump replacing the White House's cyber director.

In the briefing, Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S. This comes after midterm election voters from both parties showed their opposition to future unfettered growth.

White House

Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout

"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off," Trump said of the massive complexes that have drawn criticism from communities due to environmental and noise pollution.

He also announced penalizations against companies that try to build data centers outside the U.S.

"If it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.

Trump's trip to China came as Trump's own cabinet on what approach to take toward China. Trump's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been in favor of selling China U.S. chips, a stance that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has expressed a more hawkish view toward China, and Trump has acknowledged both perspectives.

The divide has become more prominent as Lutnick and Trump face backlash for their relationship to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from his position after admitting to an affair with a woman who may be a Chinese spy.

On Friday, Trump said he only wants "older chips" to be sold to China, rather than the most cutting-edge technology the U.S. has, and he said he'd be OK with no chips going to China at all, though he pointed out the downside to that.

"You have to understand, China makes chips too," Trump said. "And if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves."

articles.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
articles.description: When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame. The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine
articles.content:
By Ben Brubaker

Staff Writer

November 20, 2026

algorithms computer science graph theory networks All topics

One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira, a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”

Think Globally, Act Locally

Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey, a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

Godfrey, Schapira, and their colleagues showed that in this model, perfect resilience isn’t always achievable. They did so by finding a single example of a network layout that can’t be made perfectly resilient. No matter what set of routing rules you choose, there’s always a pattern of link failures that will cause some packets to get stuck in a loop.

But the network they identified was fairly complicated. Was it a rare example? Or is perfect resilience impossible in many other networks as well?

Minor Problems

The 2012 paper caught the attention of Stefan Schmid, a networking researcher now at the Technical University of Berlin. He toyed with the perfect-resilience problem on and off for years, but his first real progress came in 2020, when he and his colleagues made a connection to a topic in mathematics called the theory of graph minors.

Computer scientists have long studied the mathematical properties of real-world networks by modeling them as graphs — webs of nodes connected by lines called edges. Imagine that you start with a graph, then repeatedly simplify it using three basic operations: You can delete a node, delete an edge, or merge pairs of connected nodes. The graphs that you can obtain by combining these operations are known as the minors of the larger graph.

Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's U.S. Senate race

Politics Nov 20, 2026 9:22 AM EST

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot.

Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.

In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground."

That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.

READ MORE: Alaska voters reject ballot measure seeking to repeal open primaries and ranked voting system

In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: "Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I'm eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans."

Messages seeking comment also were left with Sen. Sullivan's campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.

The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump's direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.

Educate your inbox

Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.

Form error message goes here.

Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm.

The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement.

Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Trump's allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.

It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states' handling of their elections.

Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government's list contained many U.S. citizens.

Riccardi reported from Denver.

articles.title: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: independents
articles.description: The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris MinnsGet our daily political email, free app or daily news podcastThe New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north sho
articles.content:
The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

  • Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

articles.title: Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie
articles.description: This year, be thankful for canned pumpkin puree.The post Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie appeared first on Popular Science.
articles.content:
It’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table. The flesh has been cooked until soft. But the hard part is still ahead. To turn the pumpkin into pie, the cook must mash it, scrape it, and force it through a sieve, separating smooth pulp from stubborn strings and fibers. There is no can of pumpkin puree. No food processor. Just the pumpkin, rudimentary kitchen tools, and a lot of elbow grease. The work could take hours, all for an eight-person dessert. An 1876 New England cookbook, for example, instructed cooks to simmer pumpkin for six to eight hours, stirring frequently, before rubbing it through a colander.

It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert. Pumpkin flesh doesn’t naturally break down into a silky puree. Cooking softens its tissues, but turning the squash into smooth filling requires additional mechanical work.

For generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle. Eventually, factories took over the work of cooking and processing pumpkins into puree. But the solution didn’t stop there. Growers also turned to pumpkin varieties with naturally smoother, less fibrous flesh, making the job easier before the squash even reached the factory.

The earliest-known pumpkin pie recipe is from 1796

Pumpkin was an important food in North America long before Thanksgiving became a national holiday. Indigenous peoples cultivated and prepared the squash in many forms, and European colonists adopted pumpkins as a plentiful crop. Colonists adapted their own pie-making traditions to the abundant squash, incorporating pumpkin into sweet and savory pies. By the 17th century, recipes for pumpkin-filled pies were appearing in English cookbooks.

In 1796, the first known American cookbook, Amelia Simmons’s American Cookery, included a recipe for “Pompkin Pudding” made with cooked pumpkin, milk, eggs, and spices. Before the pumpkin could be combined with the other ingredients, the recipe called for it to be strained, separating fine pulp from tougher material. 

When did Thanksgiving become a national holiday?

Thanksgiving didn’t take shape as a national tradition until the mid-19th century. Pumpkins were harvested in the fall and could be stored through the colder months, making them a natural ingredient for a holiday associated with the autumn harvest.

The story of the Pilgrims sitting down with Native Americans for the first Thanksgiving has some truth to it, too. In 1621, English colonists and members of the Wampanoag people did gather for a three-day harvest celebration. But the friendly, feel-good version passed down in schoolbooks leaves out a much more complicated history of colonialism and conflict.

It wasn’t until over two centuries later that Sarah Josepha Hale, a prominent magazine editor, campaigned for decades for a national holiday, and, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “day of Thanksgiving.” She believed a shared day of gratitude, centered on family and community, could help unite a country increasingly divided by political conflict.

Hale also helped popularize the foods associated with the holiday, promoting a traditional New England Thanksgiving menu through her magazine. Pumpkin pie was already a regional favorite, but as Thanksgiving spread nationally after the Civil War, the dessert became part of the broader American tradition.

Pumpkin pie became increasingly associated with the holiday meal during this era, drawing on its roots in New England’s seasonal cooking traditions. Preparing it remained labor-intensive, and results varied.

When did factories start making pumpkin puree?

Industrial food processing offered a solution to the labor-intensive process of making pumpkin pie. Factories could cook and mechanically break down pumpkin in large quantities, producing puree without requiring every household to repeat the tedious process. Canning transformed pumpkin from a seasonal ingredient demanding considerable preparation into a convenient product that could be stored and used when needed.

John Coupland, Ph.D., professor of food science at Penn State, describes the work involved in preparing pumpkin by hand as “astonishing.” Industrial processing made pie filling far more convenient, eliminating the need to cook, mash, and strain a pumpkin from scratch. 

It also gave bakers a reliable starting point, helping make pumpkin pie more consistent and cementing its place at the Thanksgiving table.

The science of smoother pumpkin

Making pumpkin puree is more complicated than simply cooking the flesh until soft. Pumpkin cells are surrounded by walls containing materials such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cooking softens the tissue, while mechanical processing breaks it into smaller particles. Together, these processes help determine the puree’s texture and moisture.

The goal is a smooth puree that is neither watery nor full of tough fibers. The pumpkin variety matters, as do the heating conditions and mechanical methods used to break down its flesh.

Modern food processing allows manufacturers to control these variables on a large scale, producing batches with similar textures and moisture levels. That predictability is especially valuable in pumpkin pie, where the filling’s consistency helps determine the finished dessert.

But the food industry found another way to improve the process: start with a pumpkin better suited to the job.

The pumpkin made for the can

That is where Libby’s, one of the country’s largest canned-pumpkin producers, and the Dickinson pumpkin enter the story.

According to Libby’s, farmer Elijah Dickinson brought special Dickinson pumpkin seeds from Kentucky to Illinois in 1835. The variety became closely associated with commercial pumpkin processing, and Libby, McNeill & Libby acquired Dickinson & Co. in 1929, strengthening the company’s connection to the crop.

Dickinson pumpkins look different from the bright orange pumpkins sold for carving (often called field pumpkins). Their tan skin matters less to processors than the dense flesh beneath it. Relatively high in solids and sugars, Dickinson pumpkins are particularly well-suited to puree.

Many carving pumpkins, by contrast, have stringier flesh that makes them harder to process into a smooth puree. Coupland explains that they are not ideally suited to commercial food production because their fibers can be difficult to break down.

Coupland describes Dickinson puree as having a “smooth, even texture,” adding that it means you won’t be “picking fibers out of your teeth.” Rather than trying to eliminate the stringiness of a carving pumpkin, processors can start with a variety whose natural characteristics make the job easier. The raw material itself becomes part of the technology.

Libby’s helped bring this approach into American kitchens through its canned-pumpkin business, pairing a suitable variety with industrial processing to deliver consistent puree to home bakers.

Interestingly, Dickinson pumpkins belong to Cucurbita moschata, a species that includes several varieties of winter squash. Many familiar carving pumpkins belong to Cucurbita pepo. Botanically, the distinction between pumpkin and squash is largely a matter of common usage rather than a strict scientific boundary. The FDA permits certain sweet, golden-fleshed squashes to be labeled as pumpkin in canned products, reflecting the longstanding overlap in how the terms are used in the food trade.

For pumpkin pie, what matters most is the flesh inside: how it tastes, how it breaks down, and how consistently it performs. Today’s Thanksgiving cooks no longer needs to work themselves to the bone because the food industry has learned to do the work first.

White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans

Politics Nov 20, 2026 8:43 AM EST

WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.

Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump's cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote in a post on X. "Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."

President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

READ MORE: Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal?

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.

The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, where he downplayed the episodes, declaring that "things like that happen."

"She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

articles.title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
articles.description: Russia launched one of its biggest air attacks yet as it rejected the prospect of security guarantees for Ukraine.
articles.content:
Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge

ByDan Woodland and Sarah Rainsford, Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent, in Kyiv
  • Published
    20 November 2026, 08:04 GMT
Updated 6 hours ago

Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.

Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.

Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".

The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.

At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.

Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".

Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.

The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.

The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.

Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.

He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.

The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.

The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.

On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.

It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.

Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.

Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.

France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.

He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.description: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
articles.content:
Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour

BySareen Habeshian
  • Published
    20 November 2026

A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

The Texas Department of Criminal Justice on Friday denied any claim that Dennes's execution was "botched", adding that the agency followed its protocols in carrying it out successfully.

"The overall process took about an hour, which is not atypical," department spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez told the BBC.

"The agency took its time to ensure the IVs were inserted into viable veins, placing them in the left foot and left side of the neck," she said, adding that the allegations of pain made by Dennes "began prior to any drugs being administered".

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.

Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

articles.title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
articles.description: The same day Dennes was given lethal injection, Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year.
articles.content:
This photo combination shows Reinaldo Dennes, left, on April 14, 2026 and Thomas Mitchell Overton. Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP hide caption

Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP

HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.

And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.

The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.

Sponsor Message

National

Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"

Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."

Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

Sponsor Message

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.

She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.

Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.

Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."

"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.

"David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."

Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."

Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

Sponsor Message

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

articles.title: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
articles.description: Congress needs to pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown next month, providing Dems an opportunity to leverage power. And, the Army says waiting to detonate lead azide could become dangerous.
articles.content:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.

Reporters set up for a press conference outside of the U.S. Capitol Building on Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Finn Gomez/Getty Images hide caption

Finn Gomez/Getty Images
  • 🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.

Sponsor Message
  • 🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.

The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.

  • 🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.
Sponsor Message

Picture show

Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption

Claire Harbage/NPR

Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

Weekend picks

Grand Theft Auto VI protagonists, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, against the backdrop of the Miami-inspired Vice City. Rockstar Games hide caption

articles.title: Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
articles.description: In a week of outages, we're thinking about the rising threat of AI-powered cyberattacks. But sometimes, it's not the most sophisticated attack that's concerning, but the easy targets buried in old software.
articles.content:
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

There is a certain thrill in spotting a dollar bill on the ground. It's free money! Well one lucky person found a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her aunt's closet, under a pile of fur coats. The Smithsonian magazine reported the painting, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I," is part of a three-part series based on Keeffe's time in northern New Mexico. O'Keeffe has described her time there as particularly impactful.

Sponsor Message

Georgia O'Keeffe's "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I" (Screenshot captured on Christie's auction page) hide caption

The woman's aunt received the painting as a graduation gift from her parents way back when. They bought it for $3,800. That's the equivalent of $42,000 in today's dollars. This week, it sold at Christie's for $4,878,000 million. Double check your closet, people.

Coming up: 

  • Why old software is so risky
  • Why Steam is pulling in less revenue from NEW games 
  • What cohost Adrian Ma is reading this week

News We're Watching

This has been a long and strange week of outages from United Airlines to Apple Pay to the F.A.A. It's got many people thinking about this seemingly omnipresent threat of cyberattack. The agencies and companies experiencing the outages insist they're unrelated to cyberattacks. But there is a lot of concern right now about how vulnerable the U.S. is to these digital threats with the combination of fast-growing AI and decidedly fragile infrastructure.

Case in point, earlier this month, Europe faced ANOTHER hack on its supermarket refrigeration. Grocery stores and butcher shops across seven countries saw their fridges and freezers turned up to more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

It wasn't some complicated, sophisticated attack. It was hackers that found a vulnerability in old software. A vulnerability that had existed for a long time.

"That's where attackers see a big opportunity," said Aaron Mitchell, CEO of HeroDevs. "That's an easy way for me to get access and start to do some real damage."

After all, there is a lot of old software out there. Ones that touch utilities, hospitals, and critical infrastructure - or airlines. In some cases, companies didn't feel much urgency to address security gaps.

Employees empty freezers after a hacker attack raised the temperature in the freezers to 50 degrees Celsius (Photo by Johan NILSSON / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images) / Sweden OUT JOHAN NILSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption

JOHAN NILSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

HeroDevs is a cybersecurity firm that does the addressing FOR companies. They help maintain support for a certain kind of software called open-source. When a software reaches end-of-life, and a company has moved on to new ideas, they might pay HeroDevs to maintain it and (importantly!!) patch vulnerabilities.

That could be more important than ever because AI is helping find a record number of these vulnerabilities. Last week, VulnCheck, a cybersecurity consulting firm, posted that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been found and disclosed so far this year, more than double than 2025. Hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities 33% faster compared to 2025.

Sponsor Message

In other words, vulnerabilities in outdated software are a prime target for hackers.

"About half of all exploits that happen, known exploits of a vulnerability, are happening on versions that are no longer supported by the maintainer," said Mitchell. "That number is rapidly growing."

This is a problem because countless websites, companies, and governments have outdated software somewhere.

Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that's built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.

"It was a huge deal, and for the whole week the whole internet was kind of on fire trying to get this thing patched," said Mitchell.

Still, in some cases, Mitchell said there were documented cases of websites that DID get exploited.

This is one example of how a small entrance for bad guys can be so dangerous. But these little doorways keep popping up. On Tuesday, an AI company revealed a critical vulnerability in Java known as Java4Shell prompting websites and companies to quickly take actions to patch against it.

As we can see and perhaps even feel, hackers are taking advantage. The most common cyberattack on utilities involves outdated software. Early this month, a cyberattack hit French blood banks, looking to increase temperatures using a similar tactic to the refrigeration hacks, although French authorities caught the attack in time and stopped it.

Richard Horne, the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said that "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long." In 2028, the UK predicts AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

For now, Aaron Mitchell says, exploitation of vulnerabilities isn't taking off as much as it could be, "but every day that goes by, we get that much closer to the edge."

Sponsor Message

Just yesterday, Axios reported President Trump's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his role. He did not want to serve an additional two-year term, leaving an important role to be filled.

Today's Indicator

We got this economics podcast before GTA VI

If you HAVEN'T listened: This is the week of Grand Theft Auto VI. The wildly hyped game has already collected more than $1.5 billion in pre-sales. But the game itself is almost like a cover charge for an entire digital world, and, importantly, economy.

"Take-Two Interactive learned from GTA V that selling a product at retail is great, but better yet, what if you could continue to sell expansions and in-game events and items over a longer term?" said Joost van Dreunen, a professor at the NYU Stern School of Business.

Banner announcing the release of the new Grand Theft Auto VI in Berlin on November 17, 2026 (Photo by RALF HIRSCHBERGER / AFP via Getty Images) RALF HIRSCHBERGER/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption

RALF HIRSCHBERGER/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

GTA VI isn't launching its story mode with micro-transactions. That will likely come with the online mode of the game, expected to be released next year. The story mode can hook players into the world, and the online mode can keep them there. THEN you might start wanting to buy a few things. In the current GTA Online, based in the previous game's world, you can buy a digital yacht for $100 real US dollars.

LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE

If you HAVE listened: Overall, Steam is doing just fine, but in 2024, new releases accounted for just 29% of Steam revenue. In 2025, 27%. This year, it's down to 21%, according to the Alinea Insight substack.

To reporter Ricky Mulvey, this means people might not want new games and GTA VI is an exception to the rule.

"What is the purpose of playing a game? Not just the coolest, most advanced graphics," Ricky said. "I want to talk to my friends"

Other reasons back catalogue items are doing well: they're a fraction of the price. Plus, who can keep up with the latest and greatest console?

Sponsor Message

Rest of the Week

  • How three archetypes determine the way influencers make their money
  • How a $5B tribal settlement could shake up Western water markets
  • Is manufacturing ever coming back to the US in a big way?

Listener Mailbag

Listener Chris Browett sent in a question from Virginia Beach, VA

Question: Longtime fan, and I really enjoyed the episode on the death of the sitcoms. I've been rewatching old shows lately and just finished White Collar. It made me realize how much I miss full length seasons. They give you something to look forward to week after week. Eight episode seasons are over before they even start. The new economics make sense for most shows, but what about the big franchises like Star Wars, where Disney earns money from licensing and merchandise anyway? More episodes would mean more material to sell around, so why not lean into longer seasons? As streaming bills creep toward a regular cable bill, do you think that math changes?

Reporter Ricky Mulvey's Response
Hi Chris! Glad you enjoyed the episode and thanks for writing in. You're kind of describing an economic concept called "marginal utility". Or how much enjoyment do you get from your tenth episode of a binge watch versus the eighth? I imagine that this is the concept that the streaming execs are looking at too.

How much more likely are you to buy a Star Wars shirt after five episodes or ten? Does it matter?

Add into this the incredible cost of some streaming shows. Disney's Andor cost more than $20 million per episode. I think these higher production costs are a key reason why you see shorter seasons too.

And I think that as streaming bills creep toward cable bills the move is to live events. Streamers are looking to give you a reason to watch live and not cancel. You've seen this with Netflix adding the WWE and the Women's World Cup in 2027, Apple adding Formula 1, and Amazon with Thursday Night Football.

Sponsor Message

Cheers,
Ricky

In Our Spare Time

Co-host Adrian Ma read The Hot Young Widows Club

Recently, I read a book that deeply resonated with me called The Hot Young Widows Club.(Okay, actually, I listened to the audiobook. But I've been assured by various totally unbiased friends that listening to audiobooks counts as reading.) This memoir by Nora McInerny, written after she lost, in quick succession, a pregnancy, her husband, and her father, is one of the sharpest articulations of grief that I've ever read (or listened to).

And somehow, amazingly, it is also funny. This book made me cry. And laugh. And very often, cry and laugh at the same time. She manages to vividly capture the soul-wrenching pain and messiness of grief, while telling it to you in a comforting, conversational style, like you're commiserating with a best-friend over bottomless cups of diner coffee. If you've lost a partner, or are wondering how to support someone who has, I think you'll find this book helpful.
